en: Jagannātha Paṇḍitarāja:
*Rasagaṅgādhara*, Chapter 1:
"Even when merely remembered, she compassionately removes the heat of youth from men."
May some indescribable rain-cloud, encircled by hundreds of flashes of lightning with unfailing luster,
clinging to the celestial trees on the banks of the Yamunā,
and kissing my mind, come to be.
The illustrious Jñānendra Bhikṣu, who mastered the entire expanse of the science of Brahman; who learned the profound doctrines of Kaṇāda and Akṣapāda from Mahendra;
and who studied the teachings of Jaimini in the city of Śiva from Devadeva himself— [he was my preceptor].
He who was the possessor of all vidyās became one whose pure speech attained the remainder of the remaining digits.
I pay homage to that great preceptor named Perubhaṭṭa, the beloved of Lakṣmī, by whose effortless play even nectar flows from a stone.
By me, submerged within the inner depths of the ocean of the afflictions of conceit,
has been raised up this jewel Gaṅgādhara, who possesses the essence of graceful aesthetic flavor;
it dispels the internal darkness and has taken its place in the hearts of the virtuous.
Let her fashion all ornaments as well, though they have lost their pride.
Let a few who stand at the forefront of the connoisseurs refine the meanings;
nevertheless, my labor will somehow not have its purpose realized.
Let these lords of whales continue to stir up the ocean.
What fruitless exertion does this cause for Mount Mandara?
Having composed a new poem here that conforms to the examples, nothing belonging to another has been placed herein;
for is the fragrance of flowers ever enjoyed even by the mind?
By the deer who possesses the power to produce musk.
Having crossed the ocean of learning by means of reflection, Paṇḍitarāja Jagannātha composes this inquiry into poetics titled *Rasagaṅgādhara* out of a sense of curiosity;
may this composition named *Rasagaṅgādhara* be victorious for a long time.
Moreover, may it delight the families of poets, which are naturally well-disposed toward it.

In this regard, since poetry— which serves numerous purposes such as fame, supreme delight, and the grace of the Guru, King, and Deity— must necessarily be defined through its qualities (guṇas), ornaments (alaṃkāras), and so forth for the sake of the proficiency of both the poet and the connoisseur, we shall first define its characteristic (lakṣaṇa); for that characteristic is the delimiting attribute (viśeṣyatāvacchedaka) of that [poetry] and the means for establishing its distinction from other things.
Poetry is a word that conveys a delightful meaning.
And "loveliness" (*ramaṇīyatā*) consists in being the object of a cognition that produces supramundane delight (*lokottarāhlāda*).

This "supramundane-ness" is a specific type of experience (*jāti-viśeṣa*), witnessed by direct perception (*anubhava-sākṣika*), which is synonymous with "wonder" (*camatkāra*) as it pertains to delight.
And the cause for that [delight] delimited by such [loveliness] is a specific cultivation (*bhāvanā-viśeṣa*) consisting of repeated mental connection (*punaḥ-punar-anusaṃdhāna*).
The joy produced by the cognition of the meaning of such sentences as "A son has been born to you" or "I shall give you wealth" does not possess transcendence;
therefore, there is no possibility of poetic status (*kāvyatva*) in those sentences.

Thus, the result is that *kāvyatva* (the nature of poetry) consists in being a word that conveys an object which is the content of an imaginative contemplation (*bhāvanā*) that produces aesthetic wonder; or, it consists in the state of being an imaginative contemplation whose object is the meaning conveyed by such a word, wherein the property of producing aesthetic wonder is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*); or, it consists simply in possessing the quality of aesthetic wonder through the relation of being a conveyor of an object that delimits the production [of that wonder] as qualified by itself.
As for what the ancients have said— "Poetry consists of word and meaning that are faultless, possessed of qualities (*guṇa*), and adorned with figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*)"—
that is now examined: the pair of word and meaning is not what is denoted by the term "poetry," because there is no evidence [for such a definition].
The poem is recited aloud; the meaning is understood from the poem;
the poem has been heard, yet the meaning was not known.
This is because, on the contrary, from such universal worldly usage (*viśvajanīna-vyavahāra*), one understands that the specific word itself is the referent of the term "poetry" (*kāvyapadārtha*).
If it is argued that the usage can be accounted for through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) applied to the word alone, this might indeed be so; yet...

If there were some more firmly established means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to prove that the power of the word "poetry" resides in the pair of word and meaning—which is what others consider to be the referent of the term "poetry"—then we might accept it;
however, we do not see such a thing.
As for the disputed statement, it is simply not to be trusted.
And this being the case, since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend the expressive power (*śakti*) of the word "poetry" as residing in the pair of word and meaning,
who indeed could prevent the expressive power from being established in the specific word itself through the aforementioned usage?
By this, the argument that "expressive power resides in both [word and meaning] because there is no decisive evidence [to the contrary]" is refuted.
Thus, since it is established that the meaning of the term "poetry" (kāvyapadārtha) is precisely a particular kind of verbal expression, it is proper to state the definition of that very thing,
and not of some arbitrarily conceived meaning of the term "poetry.
This same principle applies even to the definitions of the Vedas, Purāṇas, and other such works.
Otherwise, this same predicament would apply there as well.

As for the claim that the very capacity to awaken aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*) is the defining factor of poetry, and that this is indistinguishable whether residing in the word or the meaning—as some have said—that is not correct.

For since even passion (*rāga*) is accepted by all theorists of poetics, such as the author of the *Dhvanyāloka*, as a manifestor of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), it would follow that it too must be included within the definition under discussion.
What more need be said? Since almost all the constituent elements of drama (*nāṭyāṅga*) are likewise [capable of evoking rasa], their inclusion [under the definition of poetry] would be unavoidable.
By this, the view that only that which is capable of awakening rasa is the object of the definition here is also refuted.
Furthermore, the ground for the application of the term "poetry" (*kāvyapada*) resides in both word and meaning.
[The word "tree" denotes] either a composite whole or each individual [tree] as sufficient [to be the denotation].
It cannot be the first [option],
because it would lead to the undesirable consequence that just as there is the conventional usage "one is not two," there would likewise be the conventional usage "a verse-line is not a poem."
Not the second [alternative],
because it would result in the application of the designation of two distinct poems to a single verse.
Therefore, just as in the case of the definitions of the Vedas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas, it is appropriate that the definition of poetry (kāvyalakṣaṇa) also resides solely in the words.
Furthermore, it is not tenable to include poetic qualities (*guṇas*), ornaments (*alaṅkāras*), and so forth within the definition [of poetry].

For instance, in the verse "The orb of the moon has risen," which is uttered by a female messenger, a woman going to meet her lover, or a woman separated from her beloved, and which intends to convey respectively the command to go, the prohibition against going, or the absence of life; or in such cases as "The sun has set," it cannot be said that this is not poetry.
For even that which is considered by others to be poetry can be described in the same way;
moreover, the "life" of poetry, which is its power to produce aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*), remains entirely unchanged.
Furthermore, properties such as being a *guṇa* or an *alaṅkāra* lack any universal applicability (*ananugama*).
Furthermore, the conventional usage of the term "defective poetry" (*duṣṭakāvya*) cannot be metaphorical (*lākṣaṇika*) in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*).

Nor can it be argued that there is no subverting factor for the usage "defective" (*duṣṭa*) when applied to something "free from defects," as one might say "the tree possesses conjunction" (*saṃyogī*) despite being devoid of conjunction in certain parts, by way of a distinction of parts (*aṃśabheda*).
Just as there is the common perception that "the tree is joined with birds at its root,

not on its branches," this verse— where the first half is poetry and the second half is not poetry— is untenable because it contradicts the natural and universal experience of people, and because it is impossible for such a distinction to exist as a non-pervasive property (*avyāpyavṛtti*).

Furthermore, it is untenable for the excellences (*guṇas*), which are attributes of the self like bravery and so forth, or for the ornaments (*alaṃkāras*), which are embellishments like necklaces and so forth, to constitute the body [of poetry].
As for the conclusion reached in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa* that "poetry consists of nothing but rasa," that is not correct.
Otherwise, poems in which substance (*vastu*) and ornament (*alaṃkāra*) are predominant would result in being non-poetry;
nor is this an acceptable consequence, as it would lead to the collapse of the tradition of the great poets (*mahākavi*).
And likewise, poets have described the falling, rising, and whirling caused by the force of a torrential stream, as well as the playful antics of monkeys, children, and the like.
Nor should it be argued that even in those cases there is some kind of contact with rasa through a certain indirect succession;
for such a contact with rasa would also exist in the statement, "The cow moves."

In cases such as "the deer runs," [the definition of rasa] would be over-extended and thus not applicable; for every object whatsoever is either a determinate cause (vibhāva), an effect (anubhāva), or a transitory emotion (vyabhicāribhāva). This is the general direction [of the argument]. And the cause of that [rasa] is solely the creative intuition (pratibhā) residing in the poet.
And that [pratibhā] is the presentation of words and meanings conducive to the composition of poetry.

And its nature as *pratibhā* is either a specific universal (*jāti*) established as the delimitor of the causality of poetry, or it is an impartite adjunct (*upādhi*). Its cause, in some cases, is the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by the grace of deities, great souls, and so forth.
In some cases, there are both specialized training and the practice of composing poetry;
however, it is not necessarily all three.
For even in the case of children and others, inspiration arises through the mere grace of a Great Being, even without those two.
In that case, one should not postulate those two [causes] belonging to another birth;
for such a postulation is cumbersome, lacks proof, and because the effect can be accounted for otherwise.

Indeed, in the world, when the status of something as a cause has been determined by a stronger means of knowledge, such as scripture, then a cause belonging to another birth is postulated through the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) in order to exclude any subsequent observed deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Otherwise, however, because of the presence of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), when determining the causality of previously established factors, there arises only the realization that [the prior claim] was an error.
Nor can it be asserted that the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) alone is the cause;

for we observe the manifestation of creative intuition (*pratibhā*) even in one who was unable to compose poetry for some time, once proficiency (*vyutpatti*) and practice (*abhyāsa*) have somehow been acquired.
Even in that case, if an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) were admitted, it would follow that the intuition (*pratibhā*) would have occurred even before those two [conditions] due to its presence.
Nor should it be argued that another unseen force must be postulated as an inhibitor of the intuition in that instance;

for there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in postulating that the already established linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) and practice (*abhyāsa*) alone are the causes of intuition, rather than postulating two such unseen forces residing in multiple locations.
Therefore, the previously mentioned path alone is superior.

The specific difference residing in *pratibhā* (intuitive genius), which pertains to such unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) as well as to such cultivation and practice (*vyutpatti-abhyāsa*), serves as the delimiting factor for the effect;
hence, there is no fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Furthermore, *pratibhā* (creative intuition) is the delimitor of the causal condition for poetry;
or rather, it is simply the specific difference within the components of *pratibhā* that constitutes distinct poetry—thus, even here, there is no such [logical fault].

Nor should it be argued that there is a deviation from positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyabhicāra*) in cases where creative intuition does not arise despite the presence of both proficiency (*vyutpatti*) and practice (*abhyāsa*).
In that regard, since there is no evidence for such a distinction between those two, [the cause] is not delimited by the delimitors of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*).
Alternatively, there is no fault because one may postulate that a specific sin acts as an obstacle (*pratibandhaka*) in that case.

Furthermore, the status of the absence of an obstacle as a cause is identical for both the proponent who maintains that the three factors—power (*śakti*), etc.—act as causes in combination, and the proponent who maintains that power alone acts as the cause.

For it is observed that when an opponent effects a paralysis of speech (*vākstambha*) lasting for several days through mantras and other means, even a poet who has composed numerous works finds his poetry fails to arise.
And that [poetic power] is fourfold, according to the distinctions of *uttamottama* (highest-of-the-high), *uttama* (high), *madhyama* (middling), and *adhama* (low).
That first type is where word and meaning, having subordinated themselves, manifest some particular intended sense.
"Kamapi" refers to the ground of aesthetic wonder (*camatkṛti*).

By this, the exclusion of the "extremely hidden" (*atigūḍha*) and the "obvious" (*sphuṭa*) suggested meanings is achieved. Furthermore, since even the suggested meaning that is a subordinate factor (*aparāṅga*) or a means to establish the expressed meaning (*vācyasiddhyaṅga*) possesses aesthetic charm, the phrase "whose own nature has been rendered secondary" (*guṇībhāvitātmānau*) is intended to signify the predominance of the suggested meaning relative to itself [the two primary types of poetry].
Example:
Though lying close by, alas, she is powerless to fulfill her desires;
yet, with eyes slightly closed, the beloved gazes at the lotus-face of her lover.
Here, there is the objective basis (*ālambana-vibhāva*), namely the hero;
the excitant cause (*uddīpana-vibhāva*), such as the private location suggested by the nearby bed;
and the ensuant (*anubhāva*), such as that kind of gazing.
From the conjunction of transitory mental states (vyabhicāribhāvas) such as languor and longing, love (rati) is manifested.
The essential nature of the objective basis (ālambana) and the other factors will be explained [later].

Nor should it be argued that here the expressed meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is solely the heroine’s desire, namely, "If he were lying down, then I would kiss his lotus-face," because by the phrase "incapable of making her desires bear fruit," it is understood that "all her desires reside in her heart"; thus, even such a desire is communicated by the word *manoratha* itself in its general form.

Nor is there any contradiction in the fact that, although the general desire is denoted by the word *manoratha* in its aspect as a mere wish, the specific desire characterized by a particular object—namely, "I would kiss her"—is suggested; for what could possibly obstruct this? It is precisely this [suggestion] that acts as the obstruction [to the claim that the charm would not exist].
Indeed, an object, even if suggested in its specific form, is unable to produce aesthetic delight (*camatkṛti*) in connoisseurs if it has already been denoted in its general form.

For the theorists of poetics (alaṃkārikas) accept that it is precisely the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya), when not embraced by the primary function of denotation (vācyavṛtti), that possesses aesthetic charm (camatkāritva).

Since the desire to kiss is beautiful only as an ensuant (anubhāva) of love, it would lack charm if it were not suggested— just like the literal expression "I kiss," which merely conveys the desire to kiss through the power of the words themselves— and because shame likewise cannot be the primary suggested meaning.
For it is impossible for that [glance], which is perceived as the delimitor of the subject (anuvādya), to constitute the primary meaning of the sentence.
Nor should it be argued that the glance qualified by "slightly closing the eyes" is what is being enjoined, and therefore it does not function as a delimitor of the subject;
because even in that case, while the slight closing of the eyes may be an effect of that [glance], the glance qualified by "slightly closing the eyes" is itself an effect of love alone.
If bashfulness (*trapā*) alone were the primary suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), it would follow that the mention of "gazing" would be rendered purposeless;

for, while gazing is a manifest emotion (*anubhāva*) of love (*rati*) through its literal function (*vācyavṛtti*), bashfulness is a manifest emotion of that same love through suggestion (*vyañjanā)*—just as the slight closing of the eyes is—and thus it is more appropriate to consider even that [bashfulness] as subordinate (*guṇībhūta*) within it.
Or, for example:
While standing in the midst of my teachers, I gently struck that lady of curved limbs with a lotus bud;
looking at me as I did so, her creeper-like eyebrows arched and she swayed while her earrings performed a slight dance.

Here, by the phrase "you were reeling," indignation—conjoined with the sense "O you who act without reflection, what improper thing have you done?"—is suggested primarily, as it serves as the locus for the finality of aesthetic relish (*carvaṇā*).
In this case, both the word and the meaning are subordinate (*guṇa*).
Or, for example:
"Even while lying upon her bed, that slender-limbed woman could not endure the contact of his breath;
now, however, she gently pushes away the beloved’s hand as it rests upon her heart.
This verse, being part of a composition I have composed, is incomplete in its current form; therefore, it is explained here only by way of illustration.

She who, as a newlywed bride lying upon her couch, had her slender limbs contract even at the mere touch of a breath, now— on the eve of her husband’s departure— rejects with her hand the hand placed upon her heart by her anxious lover, due to the natural disposition of a new bride.
However, it is slow;

here, by means of a slow suggestion (mandākṣepa) consisting in the gradual attainment of its own locus, the permanent emotion (sthāyibhāva) called love (rati) is manifested through a perceptible sequence (saṃlakṣyakrama). And it will be demonstrated that even the permanent emotions and other such elements can be suggested with a perceptible sequence.
And they designate this very distinction as *dhvani*.

As for the verse "niḥśeṣacyutacandanaṃ... which was explained by Appayya Dīkṣita in the *Citramīmāṃsā* in the context of examples of *dhvani*: the inclusion of the word "entirely" (*niḥśeṣa*) is intended to rule out the alternative possibility that the removal of the sandalwood paste was accomplished otherwise, namely, by the pulling of the upper garment.
Therefore, by excluding the possibility that the falling of the sandalwood paste occurred during a common bath, the mention of the "slope" (taṭa) serves to reveal the marks of sexual enjoyment;
for while sandalwood paste might fall everywhere during a bath,
in your case it is seen only upon the upper part of the slope of your breasts.
This [description] is produced solely by the act of embracing.

Likewise, regarding the phrase "the lip has its redness rubbed away," the mention of "lip" (*adhara*) specifically serves to reveal the mark of sexual enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*). This is done to exclude the possibility of an alternative explanation—that the slight fading of the previous color was merely due to the delay in taking betel—and to establish that the rubbing away of the color is common to both bathing and lovemaking. Thus, by specifying "lip," the sign of sexual union is disclosed.
By the passage beginning with, "On the upper lip, which still possesses passion, the mere lower lip has its passion wiped away— this is caused solely by the act of kissing," and ending with,

"This too is an example of *dhvani*," [the author shows that] sentence-meanings composed of elements such as the riverbank (*taṭa*) provide assistance in manifesting the primary suggested meaning (*pradhānavyaṅgya*) by means of excluding bathing and thereby establishing the limbs of sexual union, such as embracing and kissing.

This [position] is based on a failure to understand the true nature of the science of poetics (*alaṃkāraśāstra*), for it contradicts all the works of the ancients and is logically inconsistent. To illustrate: at the end of the fifth chapter (*ullāsa*), [it is stated that] "in the verse beginning with *niḥśeṣa*, those things such as the falling away of sandalwood paste which are presented as indicators (*gamaka*) [of a lover’s departure] can also occur due to other causes."

Furthermore, the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* has stated that because these [objects] are employed here specifically for the purpose of bathing, they are not restricted solely to enjoyment, and thus they are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Likewise, he says regarding that very same point:
"O pious man, wander about with confidence; that dog has been killed by him today."
In such passages as "by the fierce lion dwelling in the thickets on the banks of the Gola river," the author of the *Vyaktiviveka*,

while rejecting the view that meaning is conveyed through inference— consisting of the knowledge of a sign (*liṅga*) and the thing signified (*liṅgin*)— admits that suggestion (*vyañjanā*) occurs even from a sign that is doubted due to being either inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*) or unestablished (*asiddha*).
And in this very way, the author of the *Dhvanyāloka* stated in the first chapter:

"Thus, there is a clear contradiction between your treatise—which seeks to establish the non-commonality [of suggestion]—and the works of authoritative scholars who demonstrate the commonality of suggestors.

Furthermore, we ask: for what purpose is this non-commonality of the suggested meaning being established through the exclusion of bathing in a pond by means of the subordinate sentence-meanings beginning with "niḥśeṣa" (without remainder)?

If it is argued that [the mention of these qualities] is for the purpose of manifesting the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), we say no; for the unique characteristics residing in the suggestor (*vyañjaka*) are not a means for manifestation. [As it is said:
"The drooping eyes, weakness, anxiety, languor, and labored breathing..."

In passages such as, “O friend, this [state] belonging to a woman of great misfortune oppresses you,” it is accepted that even common qualities like insomnia (*aujjnidya*) and so forth function as suggestors of specific meanings by virtue of the particularity of the speaker and other factors;
on the contrary, because uniqueness— which is synonymous with universal concomitance (*vyāpti*)— is conducive to inference (*anumāna*) and thus opposed to suggestion (*vyañjanā*).

If it is argued that even though [the body] is composed of parts such as the banks [of a pond], the meanings of sentences such as "without remainder" (*niḥśeṣa*) and so forth do not lack commonality [with other cases], because such [results] could also occur through wiping with a cloth moistened with water and the like—then what human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) is served by excluding bathing in a pond?
For just as inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) in a single instance is contrary to inference, so too is inconclusiveness in many instances; moreover, it is not contrary to the individual [instance].

Moreover, in this case, within the body of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), two elements constitute the whole: the act of going to her presence and the aspect of the result, which is the act of dalliance.
Now, according to your own view, it is difficult to establish that the portion "you went to her presence" is itself suggested;

for, according to the method you have stated, the meanings of the qualifying phrases—such as "without remainder" and so forth—are subsumed under the expressed meaning (*vācya*), namely, the act of bathing in the pond.

Or rather, because [the literal meaning] is sublated, it is logical that the negation and the affirmation are understood through the indication of contraries by the two words "gone" and "not gone," which express the primary sentence-meanings consisting of affirmation and negation residing in the level of the expressed meaning (*vācyakakṣā*).
For when a meaning has been revealed through the sublation of the primary sense, it is not appropriate for it to be cognized through direct denotation (*vyakti*).

For example, in the case of "Aho! Full is the lake where men roll and bathe," there is an implication (*ullāsa*) dependent on the impossibility of the qualification of the agent (*kartṛviśeṣaṇa*) in the absence of fullness.

Now, if it is argued that even though going near her is understood through indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the aspect of the fruit—namely, sexual dalliance—is nonetheless unimpededly understood through suggestion (*dhvanana*) based on the power of the indicated meaning (*lakṣyaśaktimūla*); [we reply:
"Lowness (*adhamatva*) is the state of being inferior, and that arises either from birth (*jāti*) or from action (*karman*)."

For in the passage beginning with "In that regard, a superior heroine does not state the inferiority of birth of the hero," you yourself have clearly stated that [the meaning] is to be known through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*).

Furthermore, you do not accept that what is obtainable from other means constitutes the literal meaning (*śabdārtha*) of a word. Moreover, even if you were to somehow admit the operation of suggestion (*vyañjanā*) here, your desired conclusion would still not be established; for the [meanings] expressed...

Furthermore, since the states of having sandalwood paste completely washed away from the slopes of the breasts and so forth, as well as the state of being "low" (adhama), cannot be accounted for by any other means according to your own stated method—being instead produced solely by the amorous encounter with the female messenger—it would follow that these are instances of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (where the suggested meaning is subordinate).
Thus, there is also a very clear contradiction with logical reasoning.
Therefore, it is more appropriate that the meanings of the qualifying clauses, as formulated by the highly clever heroine, possess a commonality with the literal meaning (*vācyārtha*).

For instance: O you who are intent on your own interests and unaware that suffering has come upon your kinsmen, out of fear of missing the time for your bath, you have gone from here to the pond to bathe, rather than going to the presence of my beloved by the river;
yet you did not go to that lowest of men, because of your ignorance of the pain of others and your nature as a giver of sorrow.
Since the sandalwood paste has fallen off entirely from the slopes of her breasts rather than from the chest itself—

because, out of bashfulness before the many young men gathered at the pond, she repeatedly rubbed them in frustration with her pair of vine-like arms joined in a *svastika* with their tips resting on both shoulders due to the height of the slopes—

it follows that the upper lip was not properly wiped clean by the haste; whereas the lower lip, by comparison, received greater friction from the rinsing water, the fingers used for cleaning the teeth, and so forth.
Furthermore, because the eyes were not properly washed, the collyrium remained only on the upper part due to contact with mere water;
and because of the cold and her physical emaciation, your body is covered in horripilation.
Thus, such a statement made by that clever woman, containing a hidden intention, was appropriate.
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of destroying the aesthetic ingenuity (*vaidagdhya*).

Thus, since these sentence-meanings are common [to all], and because there is no sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*), the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*) is not immediately apprehended; so how could there be any occasion for indication (*lakṣaṇā*) here?
And subsequently, once the expressed meaning has been understood, when the specific qualities (*vaiśiṣṭya*) of the speaker, the person addressed, the hero (*nāyaka*), and so forth, are perceived...

The established conclusion of the Alaṃkārika school is as follows: when the subordinate word (*adhamapada*) is present, the common attribute— the quality of being a giver of pain that motivates one's own action— residing in the denoted meaning (*vācyārtha*), which exists in the form of being a giver of pain caused by another offense, culminates through the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*) in the form of being a giver of pain caused by the lover’s union with the female messenger (*dūtī*).
By this it is meant: "Inferiority is the state of being base, and that occurs either by birth or by action.

Among these, a superior heroine does not speak of her hero's inferiority by way of birth, nor of any action other than base actions such as union with a messenger girl, which result from her own transgressions."

As for what was stated— that such a thing, having already been endured prior to the dispatching of the messenger, is not fit to be disclosed and thus, by process of elimination, results in nothing other than sexual union— that too is refuted.

This is because it would be utterly improper for a clever and excellent heroine to clearly disclose her own hero’s offense—namely, his enjoyment of another woman—in the presence of her friends; rather, she intends to convey to the messenger that even those past offenses which were previously endured have now become unbearable. This is the general direction of the argument.
That second [type] is where the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya), being indeed subordinate, is the cause of aesthetic wonder (camatkāra).

The restriction [in the definition] is intended to exclude over-extension (ativyāpti) by taking another suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) that has become subordinate in relation to the expressed meaning (vācya), while the primary suggested meaning remains subordinate.
By this, such a case possesses only the status of *dhvani*.

The phrase beginning with "camatkāra" (aesthetic wonder) is used to exclude the over-extension [of the definition] to *līnavyaṅgya* (where the suggestion is submerged) and *vācyacitra* (where the expressed meaning is the ornament).

As for the fact that the commentators on the *Kāvyaprakāśa* have provided the qualification "distinct from *citra*" in the definition beginning with "that which is not such [as the former] is *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*," that is incorrect;
for it would result in the fallacy of under-extension (*avyāpti*) to those poems where *paryāyokta*, *samāsokti*, and so forth are the primary elements.
This is because all theorists of poetics agree that these possess both the status of having a subordinate suggestion (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgyatā*) and the quality of being *citra*.
The example is as follows:
"On the peaks of the Sahya mountain, scorched by the flames of Rāghava’s separation,
the monkeys, sleeping comfortably in the cool season, grow angry with the son of the Wind."

In this case, although the suggested meaning—that Rāghava has been cooled by the report of Jānaki’s welfare—is subordinated because it serves as the justification for the sudden anger directed at Hanumān by the monkey, it nevertheless possesses an indescribable charm, like a queen experiencing slavery through the force of misfortune.

Now, one might object: "Was it not previously stated that even the languor resulting from the *ākṣepa* (interruption), being inconsistent with the nature of a new bride, is established only by the suggested meaning; how then can that [languor] be considered the highest of the high?"

If it is argued that this refers to poetry (*kāvya*), we say no; for this languor, which is rendered possible even by daily friendly advice and the like— though they lack great charm— is unable, without revealing the love-in-separation (*vipralambha-rati*) that first touched the heart, to independently become an object of relish (*carvaṇā*) consisting in the bliss of another.

In this very way, in verses such as "ittham eva niḥśeṣacyutacandanaṃ," the expressed meanings—such as inferiority and so forth—which have their forms initially established by a meaning other than the suggested one, serve as suggestors; thus, there is no subordination (*guṇībhāva*) even in those cases.

Between these two types [of suggestion], which possess an undeniable aesthetic charm, there exists a certain distinction perceivable by the connoisseurs (*sahr̥daya*) based on predominance and non-predominance.
As for that which was stated by the author of the *Citramīmāṃsā*:
"Will you come here, my beloved, at the end of the watch, or at midday, or even later than that? Or perhaps when the entire day has passed?"—
thus [she speaks] to her lover who desires to go to a land reachable only after hundreds of days.
He carries away my movement with the childish prattle [of my children], accompanied by tears and falling water.

In this [verse], "the entire day" is the ultimate limit; beyond that, the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*)—"I am unable to sustain my life"—is a subordinate element (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*) because it serves as a means for establishing the expressed meaning (*vācya*), which consists in the prevention of the beloved’s departure.
This is not correct.

For the very words of the speech beginning with "at the end of the watch, with tears falling from their eyes," etc., serve as the means for establishing the expressed meaning—the prevention of the beloved’s departure—and thus there is no subordination of the suggested sense.

Because by the instrumental case in the word *ālāpaiḥ* ("by means of conversations"), the fact that the primary meaning [of "conversation"] serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the action of "taking away" is clearly understood.

Nor should it be argued that what was stated [in the previous verse]—that even a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) can serve as a factor for the establishment of the expressed (*vācyasiddhyaṅga*)—is not possible here;

for in cases such as *niḥśeṣacyutacandanam*, since the suggested meaning (the lover's enjoyment of the messenger) could serve as a factor for establishing the expressed meaning (her low character), it would result in the suggested meaning becoming subordinate (*guṇībhāva*).

Or, even if it be granted that he is unable to sustain his life beyond that point, and thus the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) becomes subordinate (guṇībhāva) because it serves as a factor for establishing the literal meaning (vācyasiddhyaṅga),

nevertheless, who could prevent its status as *dhvani*? For it is manifested through the union of the excitant (*vibhāva*) such as the hero and others, the ensuant (*anubhāva*) such as tears and the like, and the transitory emotion (*saṃcārin*) such as mental agitation, all of which constitute the state of separation-in-love (*vipralambha*).
That in which the aesthetic charm of the expressed meaning does not reside in the same locus as the aesthetic charm of the suggested meaning is the third [type].

As in the description of the Yamunā: “She is a friend of the blessed Bhāgīrathī, who, while searching for her son Maināka, acted as an arm of the Himālaya mountain that had entered the belly of the ocean.

Here, the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) alone is the cause of aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*), even though it is merely suggested (*vācyā*). Although a slight charm exists in [the qualities of] whiteness and reaching down to the bottom of the underworld (*pātāla*), it is submerged within the belly of the charm of the poetic fancy and swallowed by the saffron paste applied to the limbs by a city-woman (*nāgarikā*) acting as a rival heroine.
Only the whiteness of her own limbs is perceived;
there is no denoted meaning (*vācyārtha*) whatsoever that is capable of producing charm by itself without even slightly touching upon the suggested sense (*pratīyamāna*).

All poetry in which figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*) predominate is included within these two varieties—the second and third—namely, those where the suggested meaning is either fully manifest (*jāgarūka*) or subordinate (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*).
That in which verbal charm, embellished by the charm of meaning, is predominant is the fourth [type], the inferior. For example:

"Salutations, repeated salutations to You—the protector of the earth (gotrātṛ), who are the protector of the lineage (gotra) of the enemy of the mountain-dweller (the lion); the enemy of the enemies of the three Vedas (the sun), whose eyes are the son of Mitra (the moon)."
Here, the aesthetic charm of meaning is subsumed within the aesthetic charm of sound.

Although it might be appropriate to count as the fifth and lowest-of-the-low among the varieties of poetry that which possesses aesthetic charm of sound while being entirely devoid of the general charm of meaning—
such as one-syllable verses, repeated half-verses, *yamaka* (paranomasia), *padmabandha* (lotus-arrangement), and so forth— [in this case, the former is present].

Nevertheless, because it does not actually possess the nature of poetry— since it is not pervaded by the general definition of poetry, which consists in words that convey a charming meaning— it has not been counted by us, even though it was composed here and there in various poems by great poets who were following the ancient tradition.
This is because one must conform to the actual state of things.
Some, disregarding even these four divisions, declare that poetry is of only three kinds—superior, middling, and inferior—based on their relative status.
In that case, it is improper to assert without distinction that both *arthacitra* (poetry with striking meaning) and *śabdacitra* (poetry with striking words) are of an inferior nature.
Because a clear distinction in quality is perceived.

For what sensitive person, being thus possessed of aesthetic discernment, would declare there to be no difference between such poetic expressions as "He emerged from his own palace, bestowing honor" and "That dust, its root severed by blood," on one hand, and expressions like "Surging at will," which are merely praised by the vulgar, on the other?

Even if there exists a gradation [of excellence], if they were to be considered a single variety, then why this stubborn insistence on a distinct classification for *dhvani* and *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*, which differ only slightly? Where there is a co-location (*aikādhikaraṇya*) of the aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*) of both word and meaning, one should apply the technical designation according to the definition, having deliberated upon their relationship as subordinate or primary.
However, in the case of equal prominence (*samaprādhānya*), it is simply the middle variety (*madhyama*).
For example:
"The joy of the intoxicated bees alighting upon the clusters of blossoming lotuses; the deliverance of the female ruddy geese whose hearts were distressed by the forest fire of grief."

“This is some kind of massing of lights, appearing from the edge of the sunrise mountain— a portent for those of a dark nature whose vision is impaired by [the darkness], yet a partiality toward the eye of those whose splendor is restored.
Here, because of the abundance of alliteration (*vṛttyanuprāsa*) and because it manifests the quality of vigor (*ojas*), the word is predominant.
Because it possesses the quality of clarity (*prasāda*), the suggested form or the expressed figure of speech (*hetvalaṃkāra*) is understood immediately thereafter;
since their aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*) is of equal magnitude, they possess equal prominence.
Among these, although *dhvani*—the supreme of the supreme—is of innumerable varieties, some of its general types are described here: *dhvani* is of two kinds.
It is based on primary denotation (abhidhā) and based on indication (lakṣaṇā).
Of these, the first is threefold,
due to the distinctions of suggestion consisting of rasa, matter (vastu), and poetic figure (alaṃkāra).

By the term *rasadhvani* (suggestion of rasa), there is the inclusion of rasa, bhāva, their semblances (*tadābhāsa*), the subsidence of bhāva (*bhāvaśānti*), the emergence of bhāva (*bhāvodita*), the conjunction of bhāvas (*bhāvasandhi*), and the commingling of bhāvas (*bhāvaśabalatva*), because this serves as an indicator for those whose sequence [of apprehension] is imperceptible.
Furthermore, the second type is twofold:
that in which the expressed meaning is transferred to another meaning (*arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya*) and that in which the expressed meaning is completely set aside (*atyantatiraskṛtavācya*).

Thus, within the fivefold nature of *dhvani*, because of its supreme loveliness, it is called *rasadhvani*; therein, *rasa* itself is first described: through poetry beautiful with a fitting and graceful arrangement, [the *rasa*] is presented; having entered the hearts of the sensitive (*sahṛdaya*), by the power of a particular imaginative realization (*bhāvanā*) aided by their own sensitivity, the ordinary qualities such as Duṣyanta’s being a lover or a woman’s being his beloved dissolve, and they are designated by the terms "extraordinary excitants" (*vibhāva*), "consequents" (*anubhāva*), and "transitory emotions" (*vyabhicāribhāva*).
By means of Śakuntalā and others as the objective causes (ālambana-kāraṇa), moonlight and others as the excitant causes (uddīpana-kāraṇa), and the shedding of tears and others as the effects (kārya).

Rasa is precisely that love and so forth, existing in the form of latent impressions previously deposited, which is brought into the field of experience by the subject— by whom the limited nature of the knower and other such innate attributes have been lost because the ignorance that veils the portion of bliss has been removed at that moment through a transcendental function manifested by the cooperation of mental reflection and other factors— and which is experienced together with the inherently self-luminous bliss of one's own true nature.
(1) And so they have said: "The permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), when manifested by those [factors] such as the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, is known as *rasa*.
"Manifested" (*vyakta*) means made the object of manifestation.
And the individual self (*vyakti*) is consciousness (*cit*) with its veil shattered.
For just as a lamp covered by a bowl illuminates the objects situated nearby and shines forth by itself once that [covering] is removed,
so too does the consciousness of the Self [illuminate] the emotions such as love when they are conjoined with the determinants (*vibhāva*) and other factors.
Since it is accepted that the properties of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) are manifested by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*),
it is not contradictory for the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth to be manifested by the witness as well— just like the horse in a dream or the silver on a seashell.

The emergence and disappearance of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) are metaphorically attributed to the emergence and disappearance of the relish (*carvaṇā*) of the manifesting excitants and so forth, or to the removal of its obscuration, just as the operation of the palate and other articulators is metaphorically attributed [to the emergence and disappearance] of the permanence of the phonemes (*varṇa*).
Because the destruction of the veil [of ignorance] has as its limit the relish (*carvaṇā*) of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth,
when that relish has ceased, the permanent emotion (*sthāyin*), though present, does not manifest because the light [of consciousness] is obscured.

Alternatively, by the power of the relish of the excitants and so forth, there arises in the sensitive spectator (*sahṛdaya*)— through the unfolding of his own innate sensitivity— a mental state whose form is the bliss of his own essential nature as conditioned by each respective permanent emotion, like the mental state of a yogi in meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
This means becoming one with that [object].
For this bliss is not common to other worldly pleasures, because it consists of the modification (vṛtti) of the infinite internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).

Thus, according to the internal consistency of the works of Abhinavagupta, Mammaṭabhaṭṭa, and others, it is established that rasa is a stable emotion (sthāyibhāva) such as love (rati), characterized by consciousness whose veil has been shattered.

In reality, however, in accordance with the internal consistency of the Śruti which will be cited, rasa is indeed consciousness itself—shattered of its veil and delimited by love and the other emotions.

In every respect, whether this [consciousness] is taken as the qualifier or the qualified within its qualified nature, its eternity and self-luminosity are established by taking the aspect of consciousness.
Taking up the element of aesthetic relish (*rati*) and so forth, as well as impermanence and the state of being manifested by others,
its "tasting" (*carvaṇā*)— as previously stated— is simply the destruction of the veil covering consciousness,
or else it is a modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) having that [relish] as its form.

And this [rasa] is distinct from the meditative absorption (samādhi) that consists in the savoring of the supreme Brahman, because its objective support is the bliss of consciousness permeated by objects such as the excitant (vibhāva) and so forth; furthermore,
it is to be cultivated through the mere operation of poetry.

If it is asked, "What is the proof for the manifestation of a portion of pleasure in this [state]?", the same objection applies: "What is the proof for its manifestation even in meditative absorption (*samādhi*)?
If it is argued that there is scriptural authority for this, such as the passage beginning, "That absolute bliss which is beyond the senses is to be grasped by the intellect," then [we reply]:
In this regard as well, there is the Vedic revelation: "He is indeed rasa; for having obtained rasa, he becomes blissful," as well as the direct perception of all sensitive connoisseurs (sahṛdayas).
There are two means of knowledge.

That which was presented in the second position as the savoring of aesthetic flavor (*rasacarvaṇā*), consisting of a mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) bearing that [aesthetic] form, is verbal (*śābdī*) because it is produced by the operation of words;
and it is of a direct nature (*aparokṣātmikā*) because its object is immediate pleasure.
"The reality [of rasa] is like the cognition produced by a sentence," so say the venerable Abhinavaguptācārya.
Bhaṭṭanāyaka, however, maintains that "if rasa were perceived as something external, it would lack aesthetic relish."
However, the cognition [of rasa] as residing within oneself is difficult to establish;
for Śakuntalā and the others cannot serve as excitants (*vibhāva*) with respect to the audience,
and because rasa and the like cannot be apprehended if they lack an excitant and thus have no objective support (*ālambana*).
Nor should it be argued that "the state of being a beloved" (*kāntātva*) is also present here as the delimitor of the common excitant (*sādhāraṇavibhāvatāvacchedaka*);

for one must necessarily include within the category of the excitant's delimitors the absence of a cognition whose qualifier is "being an illicit woman" (*agamyātva*)—a cognition that is not accompanied by a certainty of invalidity—and which has as its counter-positive a relation delimited by the objective relation (*viśeṣyatā*).
Otherwise, even one's own sister and others would incur the status of being an "illicit woman" through the [mere] attribute of being a "beloved."
Thus, the absence of such knowledge regarding the lack of grief, the state of being a base man, and so forth, [is required] in the case of the rasa of compassion and the like;
however, the non-arising of such knowledge is difficult to establish without defining some other obstructing factor.
If it is argued that the cognition of one's own self as non-different from Duṣyanta and others is precisely that [obstructing factor], we say no.

Because the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)—such as the hero’s being the pillar of the earth and his fortitude, versus one’s own modernity and worthlessness—is so clearly perceived, a cognition of non-difference is simply difficult to achieve.
Furthermore, what kind of cognition is this?
If it is argued that it is verbal (*śābdī*) because no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is present, we say no.
For this [cognition] would also result in being unpleasant, just like the cognitions of the narrative of a hero and heroine produced by other conventional words;
nor is it mental,
because its distinctness is perceived from the mental apprehension of those very same objects brought forth by reflection.
Nor is there memory [of such qualities],
because they were not previously experienced in that way.

Therefore, the word-meanings (padārthas) presented by the denotative function (abhidhā) are established— by means of the function of evocation (bhāvakatva)— through the prevention of cognitions of factors incompatible with the aesthetic flavor (rasa), such as unapproachability, and by way of bringing forward attributes favorable to the flavor, such as loveliness.
Thus, when the place, time, age, state, and so forth of Duṣyanta and Śakuntalā have been made common [to all],

and when the power of the prior operation has been eclipsed by the power of the third operation— which consists in the production of enjoyment— the qualities of rajas and tamas are swallowed up, and there arises, through the predominance of sattva, a resting in the bliss of one's own conscious nature.

The permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), such as love (*rati*) and so forth, which has been made an object through direct perception and brought forth by cultivation, possessing a universal nature, is the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
In that regard, both the love and other emotions being experienced, or the experience of love and other emotions, is itself the *rasa*.
Thus, this enjoyment (*bhoga*), because it is saturated with the objects [of poetry], is said to exist in close proximity to the savoring of Brahman (*brahmāsvāda*).
And so, they say that there are three components of poetry: "the denotation (*abhidhā*), the creative realization (*bhāvanā*), and the enjoyment thereof (*tadbhogīkṛti*).
The distinction of this view from the previous one lies solely in its acceptance of a separate function called *bhāvakatva* (the act of making one a connoisseur).
Experience, however, is manifestation;
and the state of being the cause of experience is not distinct from manifestation.
But that very path is different.

(3) The Neo-Naiyāyikas, however, maintain that when the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth are manifested by the poet in poetry or by the actor in drama, and once the love of Śakuntalā and others has been apprehended in Duṣyanta and the like through the operation of suggestion (*vyañjanā*), there immediately follows— by the power of a defect consisting of a specific kind of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) aroused in the connoisseur— a state in which one's own self, though delimited by ignorance, is veiled by the imagined nature of being Duṣyanta, just as a piece of mother-of-pearl [is mistaken for silver].

Like a fragment of silver appearing [in a mother-of-pearl shell], rasa is that very love and so forth directed toward an object such as Śakuntalā, which is indefinable and manifested by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin).
And this [rasa] is the effect of a particular excellence [of the causes]; it is that which is to be destroyed by a particular defect, and that which is to be produced by its removal.
Because it does not grasp its distinction from the supramundane bliss that arises immediately after it, it is designated by the term "pleasure" (*sukha*).

Alternatively, because it does not grasp the passion (*rati*) and so forth that were present prior to it, or because of the determination of identity with that passion, it is called both "suggested" (*vyaṅgya*) and "to be described" (*varṇanīya*).
Even the state of being Duṣyanta, which acts as a veil, is indeed indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*).
And "obscuring" (avacchādakatva) consists in being the delimiting factor of the substantive (viśeṣyatāvacchedakatva) in a cognition qualified by love and so forth.
By this [it is shown that] love and so forth residing in Duṣyanta and others cannot be aesthetic relish (anāsvādya), and thus they do not constitute rasa.
But how can that [love] residing in [the actor] himself be manifested by Śakuntalā and others, who are not related to him?
The argument that the cognition of non-difference between oneself and Duṣyanta and so forth is sublated by a contrary cognition has been refuted.

Furthermore, as for the "universalization" (*sādhāraṇya*) of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and other factors mentioned by the ancients, that too is difficult to establish unless one assumes some specific defect in the Śakuntalā and others who are presented through poetic words such as "Śakuntalā," which generate cognitions qualified by the property of being Śakuntalā and so forth.

Therefore, since a specific type of defect must necessarily be postulated, by that very [defect] the cognition of non-difference between Duṣyanta and others within one's own self is also easily established.

But even so, let it be granted that *rati* (erotic passion) produces a particular pleasure both in Duṣyanta and in the sensitive spectator (*sahṛdaya*); however, in the case of the *karuṇa-rasa* (pathetic sentiment) and others, how can this be, given that the permanent emotion (*sthāyin*) such as sorrow (*śoka*) is well known to be a producer of pain?
[The objection that poetry] causes delight to the connoisseur is refuted;
on the contrary, it is more appropriate that it produces suffering even in the connoisseur, just as it does in the hero.
Nor is it established that real sorrow and the like cause suffering, while imagined ones do not; thus, the suffering belongs to the heroes alone.
If it is argued that this does not apply to the connoisseur (*sahṛdaya*),
because it would follow that a rope-snake and the like could not produce fear, trembling, and so forth [in him],
and because it would be illogical for even *rati* (erotic sentiment) to produce pleasure in a connoisseur since it too is imagined (*kalpita*).
True.

If, as is evidenced by the experience of sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*), there is indeed nothing but pure bliss arising even from poems dominated by the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa-rasa*)— just as from those dominated by the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*)—
then, since a cause must be postulated in accordance with its effect, it follows that it is the extraordinary poetic operation itself that is the cause of this bliss.
Likewise, the state of being an obstacle to suffering must also be postulated.
However, if suffering, just like pleasure, is established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), then its status as an obstacle need not be postulated;
both will arise by virtue of their respective causes.
Now, how did the activity of poets arise there to compose [works], and that of connoisseurs to listen?
If it is argued that desisting is appropriate because [the act] is a means to an undesirable end, we reply: no,
because since the desirable is greater and the undesirable is less, engagement is justified, as in the case of anointing oneself with sandalwood paste.
But for those who maintain that [liberation] consists solely of bliss, activity is entirely unimpeded;
even the shedding of tears and so forth arise from the very nature of experiencing various forms of bliss,
and not from suffering.
For this very reason, it is logical that devotees of the Blessed One experience the shedding of tears and so forth upon hearing descriptions of the Blessed One;
for in that case, there is never any actual experience of suffering.

Nor, if aesthetic delight were to arise from the rasa of compassion and the like through the superimposition of identity with Daśaratha or others who possess grief within one's own self, then such delight would also occur during dreams or in cases of physical illness (saṃnipāta) when one likewise superimposes such identity upon oneself.
And since there is only suffering experienced therein,
it must be said that the same applies here as well;
for this is the greatness of the transcendent activity of poetry.
For even objects such as grief, which are normally unpleasant, produce a non-worldly delight when they are employed [as themes in poetry].
Indeed, the aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*) born from the operation of poetry is of a distinct nature compared to experience produced by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
And its being "produced" consists in its having as its object a state of passion (*rati*) and so forth, which is itself produced by a latent impression (*bhāvanā*) generated by that [relish].
Therefore, they say: "There is no harm even if the tasting of rasa (*rasāsvāda*) is not produced by the function of poetry (*kāvyavyāpāra*).
As for the arising of the cognition that [Śakuntalā] is unapproachable and so forth, this is obstructed within oneself by the notion of non-difference from Duṣyanta and others.
(4) Others, however, [hold that] through the function of manifestation (*vyañjanavyāpāra*), there is the theory of the manifestation of the indescribable (*anirvacanīyakhyāti*).

Even if [the identity between the spectator and the character] is not admitted, by the force of the previously mentioned defects, there arises a mental cognition—possessing a unique objectivity—that apprehends an identity with Duṣyanta and others, and which consists in the non-difference from the love and so forth directed toward Śakuntalā and others;

however, such a cognition occurring in dreams and the like is not born from the contemplation of the meaning of poetry, and thus it is not *rasa*. Consequently, the aforementioned aesthetic delight does not occur therein.
Even so, how indeed could there be an experience of love and the like that do not exist within oneself?
Not so;
for this is not a worldly direct perception (*laukika-sākṣātkāra*) of love and the like.
They also say: "It is not the case that the actual existence of an object must necessarily be depended upon;
rather, it is an illusion.
The conventional designation of 'having rasa as its object' for aesthetic relish (āsvādana), however, is based on its having love (rati) and so forth as its objects."

And by these [cognitions], there occurs: (1) a cognition that apprehends the qualification of love directed toward Śakuntalā and others, within one's own self, as delimited by the property of being Duṣyanta;
(2) a cognition that apprehends the identity of Duṣyanta—qualified by love directed toward Śakuntalā and others—with one's own self, which is qualified by the nature of being one's own self;
and (3) a cognition that apprehends the mutual qualification of the state of being Duṣyanta and the love directed toward Śakuntalā, both of which are qualified by the nature of being one's own self.
Alternatively, even the threefold cognition must be accepted as having rasa as its object.

In that regard, since the *rati* (erotic passion), which serves as the qualifier, is not perceived from the words, and since the manifestation (*vyañjanā*) that conveys it is not admitted [as a separate means], there is first an inference—based on signs such as gestures—for the sake of knowing the qualifier. Primarily, the rasa, such as *rati*, residing in Duṣyanta and others, is directly realized by being superimposed upon the actor who plays the role of Duṣyanta and so forth, and who is skilled in demonstrating the representation of the lovely excitants (*vibhāva*) and other factors.
Thus say some.

According to this view, the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) takes the form: "This Duṣyanta possesses a passion directed toward Śakuntalā and others," and so forth; as before, it is worldly (*laukika*) with respect to the objective substratum (*dharmyaṃśa*), but non-worldly (*alaukika*) with respect to the superimposed element (*āropyāṃśa*).

The passion and so forth residing in Duṣyanta and others [are perceived] in the actor (*naṭa*), who is apprehended as being Duṣyanta, by means of the artificial excitants (*vibhāva*) and other factors.

Others hold that "rasa is that which is inferred by the apparatus of inference (*anumiti-sāmagrī*), because of its superior strength, even when the objects [of perception] are apprehended as being non-artificial.

(7) Some maintain that "the three—vibhāva and so forth—when combined, constitute rasa. (8) Many argue that "among these three, only that which produces aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) is rasa; otherwise, even all three together are not [rasa]. (9)
“Others hold that when the determinants (*vibhāva*) are cultivated, they themselves become the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
(10) Likewise, others maintain that it is the consequents (*anubhāva*) that do so. (11) Still others say that it is the transitory states (*vyabhicārin*) alone that thus transform.”

In this regard, the aphorism—"From the conjunction of the determinants (*vibhāva*), the consequents (*anubhāva*), and the transitory states (*vyabhicārin*), there is the production of rasa"—is explained according to various philosophical views.

According to the first [view]: "From the conjunction—that is, the manifestation—of the determinants, the consequents, and the transitory states, there is the 'production' of rasa, which consists of the permanent emotion (*sthāyin*) characterized by consciousness and bliss, or rather, which consists of consciousness and bliss as manifested through that permanent emotion; this means its manifestation in its own essential form."

"In the second [chapter], it is stated: 'Through the conjunction of the determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*vyabhicārin*) by way of their perfect commonality, and through the operation of the spectator as a *bhāvaka* (one who brings to being), there occurs the production of rasa— which consists of the bliss of one's own self manifested by the surge of *sattva* supported by the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*)— and its being made an object of experience through a direct perception termed 'enjoyment' (*bhoga*')."

In the third [chapter], it is stated: "The production—that is, the arising—of rasa, which consists of the indefinable love of Duṣyanta and so forth, results from the conjunction of the determinants (vibhāva), the consequents (anubhāva), and the transitory states (vyabhicārin), due to a specific defect consisting of a particular mental impression (bhāvanā).

In the fourth, it is stated: "The production—that is, the arising—of rasa, which consists of a specific cognition, results from the conjunction—that is, the knowledge—of the determinants and so forth.
In the fifth, it is stated: "The production—that is, the superimposition—of rasa, such as love and so forth, results from the connection of the determinants and so forth."

"In the sixth [chapter], it is stated: 'The production—meaning the inference—of rasa, such as love (rati) and so forth, occurs through the conjunction with the excitants (vibhāva) and other factors, which, though artificial, are apprehended as if they were non-artificial; the subject (pakṣa) is the actor and so forth.
In the seventh: 'The designation "rasa" is applied when there is the production of rasa from the conjunction—that is, the collection—of the three, namely the excitants and the others.
In the eighth: '[It arises] from the wonder resulting from the perfect conjunction within the excitants and the others.'"
Thus, in these three views, there is a contradiction with the Sūtra.

Since the excitants (*vibhāva*), ensuants (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*vyabhicārin*) are each common to other aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*), it is impossible for any one of them alone to manifest a specific rasa; therefore, they are mentioned in combination in the Sūtra.

And so, since their combined manifestation is established as authoritative, wherever the awakening of a rasa occurs from only one of them—provided it is unique—the other two must be understood by implication.
Therefore, there is no inconclusiveness.

Thus, although this aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is determined by the wise to have various forms through diverse types of intellectual insights, it is beyond dispute that, being invariably concomitant with supreme delight, it brings about charm within this phenomenal world (*prapañca*).
And it is said: "The erotic, the pathetic, the peaceful, the furious, the heroic, the marvelous, as well as the comic, the terrible, and the loathsome— these are the nine."
Thus, by this statement, it is ninefold;
and here, the word of the Sage is the authority.
However, some say—

"Because tranquility (*śānta*) is to be accomplished through calmness (*śama*), and because that [calmness] is impossible in drama (*naṭa*), there are only eight aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) in drama; the tranquil flavor is not applicable therein," so they say. But others do not accept this.
For instance, the reason "because there is an absence of tranquility (*śama*) in the actor" is incoherent;
this is because the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in the actor is not admitted,
and because there is no obstacle to the arousal of rasa in the spectators (*sāmājika*), who possess tranquility.
Nor should it be argued that because the actor lacks tranquility (*śama*), his manifestation of those [emotions] through performance is untenable;
for in that case, since the actor likewise lacks fear, anger, and so forth, it would follow that his manifestation of those performances would also be inconsistent.

And if, despite the impossibility of the production of actual effects such as killing or binding due to the actor’s absence of anger and so forth, there is the production of artificial effects resulting from training and practice, then...
If it is observed that [the rasa] is obstructed, then the same applies to the case at hand as well.

Now, if it is argued: "Since there exist opposing elements such as song and instrumental music in drama, how can there be an intensification of the *śānta* (quiescent) rasa—which consists of aversion toward sense objects—even among the members of the audience? [then the answer follows:]
For those who accept the presence of the *śānta* rasa in drama, its opposition to song, instrumental music, and so forth [in that context] cannot be postulated on the strength of empirical evidence;

for if one were to admit that the mere general thought of worldly objects (*viṣaya-cintā*) is opposed to it, then its objective basis (*ālambana*), namely the impermanence of saṃsāra, as well as its excitants (*uddīpana*)— such as listening to the Purāṇas, the company of the virtuous, and visiting sacred groves and pilgrimage sites—
would also necessarily be considered opposed to it, since these too are objects.
For this very reason, in the final chapter of the *Saṅgītaratnākara*, it is said:
"Some have asserted that there are only eight rasas in dramatic performances; that is incorrect, because an actor does not relish any rasa at all."

By such statements, it has been established that the *śānta* (peaceful) rasa also exists in drama (*nāṭya*). Even by those who maintain that the *śānta* rasa does not exist in drama, this [rasa] must necessarily be accepted in poetry (*kāvyā*), because there is no subverting evidence against it, and because it is established by the experience of all people that literary works such as the *Mahābhārata* primarily consist of the *śānta* rasa.

In this very context, having begun with the statement, "Eight aesthetic sentiments (rasas) are traditionally taught in drama," Mammaṭabhaṭṭa likewise concluded by stating, "The peaceful (śānta) is also the ninth sentiment.
And regarding these [sentiments]:
"Love, sorrow, world-weariness, anger, energy, and wonder..."

"Laughter, fear, and disgust—these are respectively the permanent moods (sthāyibhāvas). Regarding the relationship between the aesthetic flavors (rasas) and the permanent moods: according to the first and second views, it is like that of a jar and the space delimited by the jar;
according to the third view, it is like that of real silver and indeterminable silver.
The distinction [of the object] from its cognition— such as that of silver and so forth— should be understood as being fourfold.
In that regard, because these entities remain stable throughout their continuity, [they appear as such].
Regarding their status as stable (sthāyitva):
it should not be argued that stability is difficult to attain for these [emotions] because they exist in the form of mental fluctuations (cittavṛtti) and are thus subject to rapid destruction;
nor should it be said that stability in the form of latent impressions (vāsanā) is over-extended to the transitory emotions (vyabhicārin).

This is because these [objects], which consist of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), possess the nature of stable entities precisely due to their repeated manifestation; however, this is not the case for transitory objects,
because their manifestation is merely like a flash of lightning.
As they say:

"That which is not interrupted by states of being, whether contradictory or non-contradictory, and which quickly brings about its own essential nature— that is the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), like a salt-mine."

"Those which abide for a long time in the mind, become connected with their attendants (*anubandhin*), and attain the state of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)— these are established here as the permanent moods (*sthāyin*).
The word "for a long time" is used to exclude the transitory moods (*vyabhicārin*).
By the attendant factors, such as the determinants (vibhāva) and so forth;
likewise—
“by those of the same and different classes.”
"The stable emotion (sthāyibhāva) is described as that which exists as long as the aesthetic flavor (rasa) persists, its form remaining unobstructed.
Some, however, state that the nature of being a stable emotion consists in being one of the [eight] primary emotions, such as love (rati) and so forth.
That is not so;
for it is accepted that when one [emotion] such as love (*rati*) has become fully developed (*prarūḍha*), another that has not yet become fully developed is a transitory emotion (*vyabhicārin*).
Being "fully developed" or "not fully developed" refers to being produced by many or few determinants (*vibhāva*) respectively.

As it is stated in the *Ratnākara*: "The permanent emotions (*sthāyibhāva*), such as love (*rati*) and the rest, arise predominantly from the determinants (*vibhāva*); those same [emotions], when produced only slightly by the determinants, are the transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*)."
And thus, when the heroic sentiment (vīrarasa) is predominant, anger is the transitory emotion; in the furious (raudra), it is energy (utsāha); and in the erotic (śṛṅgāra), it is laughter (hāsa).
And [the *vibhāva*] is also *nāntarīyaka* (inseparable).

However, when that [subsidiary *vibhāva*] is also produced from many *vibhāvas* for the sake of nourishing the primary [sentiment], then it should be understood as a *rasālaṃkāra* (ornament of sentiment), and so forth.
In that regard—
Rati is the specific mental state called love, characterized by mutual dependence between a man and a woman, and it is the permanent emotion (sthāyibhāva).
The mental support consisting of the guru, deities, sons, and so forth, is subject to deviation.
Grief (*śoka*) is a specific modification of the mind characterized by despondency, arising from such things as separation from or the death of a son and others.

In the case of the separation of a man and woman, while they are still alive, the predominant element is *rati* (erotic love) as nourished by agitation (*vaiklavya*); therefore, the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiment is present under the name of *vipralambha* (love-in-separation).
Here, agitation is merely a transitory emotion (*saṃcāribhāva*).
However, in the state where death has been realized, it is the agitation nourished by *rati* that predominates; thus, it is simply the *karuṇa* (pathetic) sentiment.
But when, despite the knowledge that [the beloved] is dead, there somehow arises through the grace of a deity or other means the knowledge of their revival,
then— because there is no absolute removal of that object of focus— it is merely *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) like a long absence,
not *karuṇa* (pathos).
As seen, for example, in Mahāśvetā’s words addressed to Candrāpīḍa;
some, however, maintain that there is here a distinct rasa called *karuṇa-vipralambha* (love-in-separation characterized by grief).
*Nirveda* (world-weariness) is born from the contemplation of the eternal and the non-eternal, and is termed detachment from sense objects.
But that which arises from domestic quarrels is transitory;
whereas the anger known as "blazing" (prajvalana) is born from supreme offenses such as the murder of one's teacher or kinsmen.
This [anger] has the destruction of others and so forth as its cause;
however, that which arises from a minor offense has harsh speech, refusal to converse, and so forth as its cause.
The distinction is that this very [latter type] is the transitory mental state (*vyabhicāribhāva*) known as indignation (*amarṣa*).
The energy known as "elevation" (aunnatya) arises from the recollection of one's own prowess, generosity, and so forth.
Astonishment, known as expansion (*vikāsa*), is born from the sight of extraordinary objects and the like.
Laughter, known as *vikāsa*, arises from the observation of changes in speech, limbs, and so forth.
Fear is that state called agitation, which arises from the sight of a tiger or similar causes and has as its object extreme misfortune.
However, when there is an absence of having the supreme misfortune as its object, that very same state of alarm (*trāsa*) is a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*).
Others, however, state the distinction between fear (*bhaya*) and alarm (*trāsa*), saying that alarm arises from portents, whereas fear arises through the medium of one's own transgression.
Disgust (*jugupsā*) is a specific modification of the mind (*cittavṛttiviśeṣa*) called doubt (*vicikitsā*), which arises from the sight of loathsome objects.

Thus, those things which in the world are well known as the causes— either by way of being the objective basis (*ālambana*) or by way of being the excitant (*uddīpana*)— of these stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*) residing in their respective heroes, are designated by the term "determinants" (*vibhāva*) when they are manifested in poetry and drama.
This is because of the etymological derivation [of the term] as "those which cause [the emotion] to be manifested";
and those which function as effects are designated by the word *anubhāva*.
Those whose existence or arising is subsequent [to the primary emotion],

or according to the etymological derivation "those which cause [the primary emotion] to be experienced," are those that accompany it; these are designated by the term *vyabhicārin* (transitory mental states).
In that regard, for the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), the man and woman are the objective determinants (*ālambana-vibhāva*).
Moonlight, spring, various groves, secret places, and so forth are the excitant determinants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*).
Beholding their faces, hearing of their qualities, praising them, and other such acts, as well as the involuntary states (*sāttvika-bhāva*), are the consequent manifestations (*anubhāva*).
Recollection, reflection, and so forth are the transitory mental states (*vyabhicārin*).
For the sentiment of compassion (*karuṇa*), the destruction of kinsmen and the like are the objective supports (*ālambana*).
The sight of things associated with them—such as their houses, horses, and ornaments—as well as hearing stories concerning them and so forth, are the excitants (*uddīpaka*).

The consequents (*anubhāvas*) are the casting of limbs, the shedding of tears, and so forth; the transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) are languor, exhaustion, delusion, despondency, anxiety, longing, dejection, and stupor.
For the *śānta* (the tranquil rasa), the world known as impermanent is the objective basis (*ālambana*).
Its excitants (*uddīpana*) are the hearing of the Vedanta, the sight of ascetic groves and hermits, and so on.
The determinants (anubhāvas) are aversion to sense objects, indifference toward enemies, friends, and so forth, and the loss of physical vigor;
the transitory mental states (vyabhicāribhāvas) are joy, madness, recollection, intelligence, and so forth.
For the Furious Sentiment (raudra-rasa), the determinant (ālambana) is a person who has committed an offense and the like.
The offense committed by that person and so forth is the excitant (*uddīpaka*).
The results such as killing or imprisonment, as well as the reddening of the eyes, biting the teeth, harsh speech, and seizing weapons, are the consequents (*anubhāva*).
Impatience, impetuosity, ferocity, restlessness, and so forth are the transitory mental states (*saṃcārin*).

Thus, it should be understood that whatever object belongs to a particular mental state (*cittavṛtti*) is its objective support (*ālambana*), and the excitants (*nimitta*) are its stimulators (*uddīpaka*). In this regard, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is of two kinds.
There are two types: union (*saṃbhoga*) and separation (*vipralambha*). The first occurs when love is delimited by the time of union;
the second occurs when it is delimited by the time of separation.
Furthermore, the union (*saṃyoga*) of a husband and wife is not a case of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*);
for even when they lie upon the same bed, if jealousy and other such emotions are present, it is described as nothing but the state of separation-in-union (*vipralambha*).
