Likewise, separation (*viyoga*) is not a case of non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).
Because the fault has already been stated,
these two— known as conjunction and disjunction— are specific modifications of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa),
which constitute the cognition: "I am joined" and "I am disjoined."
Among these, the first is as explained in the verse, “Though lying close by, she was powerless,” where it is established [as *rasavadalaṅkāra*].
As for what is stated in the *Citramīmāṃsā* regarding the verse, “Like word and meaning, they are joined together,” that refers to *rasadhvani*.
This [criticism] is based on a failure to perceive the path of suggestion (*dhvani*);

for in this poem, where the primary subject is the love between Pārvatī and the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), unsurpassed love is merely subordinate (*guṇībhūta*). Indeed, it is not logical that a sentiment such as *rati* (love) which has become subordinate should serve as the basis for the designation of a "suggestion of rasa" (*rasadhvani*).
This is because of the established doctrine that "the *rasa* and other [factors] stand as distinct from the ornaments (*alaṃkāra*), by virtue of being the objects to be ornamented.
An example of the second [type] is as follows:
"When the people at the time of departure chatter many auspicious words..."
With her lotus-face placed at the opening of the window of the pleasure-palace,
her breasts moist with tears falling upon her lower lip which is parched by her sighs,
the young girl with tremulous eyes gazes, alas, alas, at the lord of her life.
Here too, there is the objective basis (ālambana), namely the hero; the consequent states (anubhāva), such as sighing and the shedding of tears;
and the transitory mental states (vyabhicārin), such as despondency, anxiety, and agitation.
Delight manifested through union becomes the cause for the designation of the *vipralambha* (erotic-in-separation) sentiment because it is delimited by the time of separation.
Or, as in:
"When the honey-dripping [glance] of the Son of Nanda became manifest..."
A certain luster, skilled in the magic of attracting all eyes;
a long sigh upon her face; a pallor upon the pair of her cheeks;
and a vacant state of mind—these appeared in the hearts of the deer-eyed women of noble lineage.
Or as it is said:
"She who formerly could never endure even the touch of the corner of the eye—
she remained silent when embraced by her departing lover."
Here too, the cessation of innate restlessness and dullness are the transitory mental states (*anubhāva* and *vyabhicāribhāva*).
The ancients designate this fivefold [state] by means of conditions such as "dwelling abroad" (*pravāsa*) and so forth;
however, since no specific distinctions are perceived among those categories—such as dwelling abroad, longing, separation, jealousy, and curses—we have not elaborated upon them.
An example of compassion is as follows:

“Having abandoned all concern for your kinsmen and cast aside your affection for the teacher’s household— alas, O son endowed with discipline, how indeed have you become a traveler on the path to the next world?”
In this case, the deceased son is the objective basis (*ālambana*);
the sight of relatives at that particular time is the excitant (*uddīpana*);
and weeping is the ensuant (*anubhāva*).
The transitory emotions (saṃcāribhāvas) include dejection and others.
An example of the Quietistic (śānta) rasa is as follows:
"Of the Malaya breeze and the Kālakūṭa poison, of the tresses of beautiful women and the coils of serpents..."
“For me, an uninterrupted state of abiding in the Supreme Self has arisen toward both the dog and my own self.
Here, the entire phenomenal world is the objective support (*ālambana*);
the experience of equality everywhere is the consequential emotion (*anubhāva*).
The [mental states] beginning with *mati* (intellection) are transitory (*saṃcārin*).

Although the mention of the low and the high in the second half-verse— after they were introduced as the high and the low in the first half-verse— brings about a violation of sequence (*kramabhaṅga*),

nevertheless, this violation of sequence is indeed a merit (*guṇa*) because it serves to illuminate that, due to the speaker being identical with Brahman, a deficiency in the knowledge of high and low has arisen.
This, however, should not be cited:
"Standing upon the sandy bank of the celestial river, having placed the seal within his eyes, he then instantly drove away all sense-objects."
"When shall I, having shaken off the inner darkness, be immersed in some state of consciousness that is exceedingly sweet, possessing the luster of a cloud in a fresh sky?

Even here, although the stable emotion of *nirveda* (world-weariness) is perceived— having the multitude of objects as its support, being intensified by the banks of celestial rivers and the like, and manifested through such signs as the closing of the eyes— nevertheless...

Since the poetic sentiment (rasa) here has the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva as its objective support (*ālambana*), it is subordinate; therefore, it cannot be the basis for designating this as a *śāntarasa-dhvani* (suggestion of the tranquil sentiment).

Furthermore, this verse was composed by me in the *Karuṇālaharī*, which is primarily devoted to devotion to the Blessed Lord; thus, it deserves to have the prominence of the dominant emotion (*bhāva*) that constitutes its primary subject.
Moreover, this vigorous composition is not conducive to the *śāntarasa*, and so it should certainly not be cited as an example thereof.

In the previous verse, however, because of the understanding of identity with that [Supreme Self] through the phrase "abiding in the Supreme Self," there is no apprehension of *rati* (erotic passion). An example of the Furious (*raudra*) sentiment is as follows:
"In the fever of immense pride surging with newly-arisen youth..."
"Let this terrible axe of mine fall mercilessly— greedy for the blood trickling from the throats of proud mountains shattered by it— as my teacher’s bow, now free from trepidation, cuts [the enemy]."

In this context, the object of reference (*ālambana*) at that time is one who broke the preceptor’s bow while being unrecognized as Rāma; for this very reason, the substantive (*viśeṣya*) is not explicitly mentioned,
because it is improper to utter the name of one who has betrayed his teacher.
Or, due to the manifestation of anger,
the breaking of the bow without hesitation— inferred from a particular sound— is the excitant;
the harsh speech is the consequent emotion.
Pride, ferocity, and so forth are the transitory emotions (*saṃcāribhāvas*).
This is the speech of Bhārgava, whose meditative absorption has been shattered by the sound of the breaking of the bow.
Furthermore, the highly elevated style (*vṛtti*) here nourishes the supreme intensity of the Furious Sentiment (*raudrarasa*).

In other instances, since the disappearance of the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) is necessary when there is remembrance of the Guru, whereas in the present case, through suggestion (*dhvanana*) based on *ajahatsvārthalakṣaṇā*,
the very heightening of pride is revealed by the word "madīyā" (mine); thus, by the clearly perceived lack of discrimination, the intensity of his anger is understood.
But this should not be cited: "Hearing the sound of the bow snapping, at that very moment his memory of the murder of his great preceptor arose; his lower lip was shaken by the force of his sighing."
"The sage, son of Jamadagni, triumphs as he hurls his glance at the best of the Raghus— a glance emitting a multitude of thick, flying sparks.
Here too, the [heroic] emotion is supported by the descendant of Raghu, who serves as the locus of the offense, and is further intensified by the hearing of the sound of the breaking of the bow.

Although anger is manifested through such external effects (anubhāva) as hissing, the flaming of the eyes, and so forth, and is stirred up by internal states (saṃcārin) such as the memory of the murder of a great preceptor, pride, and ferocity,

it nevertheless remains subordinate to the poet’s aesthetic delight (kavirati), which serves as the seed for describing its power; thus, it does not constitute the basis for designating this as the suggestion of the Furious Sentiment (raudrarasa-dhvani).

However, in the example of the Furious Sentiment (*raudrarasa*) found in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, namely the verse "By whom this heinous crime was committed, approved, or witnessed," there is no expressive mode (*vṛtti*) capable of manifesting the Furious Sentiment; therefore, this is simply a lack of skill on the part of that poet. The Heroic Sentiment (*vīra*) is fourfold.
Because energy (*utsāha*), which is conditioned by these factors, is fourfold— consisting of generosity, compassion, battle, and duty—
the first is as follows:
"How much more is this [already] mine, that I should give to a twice-born who comes as a petitioner?"
“I offer my armor, most delightful to the eye, and my earrings;
having mercilessly severed [my head] with a sword,
I present my crown, from which a thick stream of blood flows forth.”
This is Karṇa’s reply to the members of the assembly who were astonished by his gift, as he was prepared to give the armor and earrings to Indra disguised as a brahmin.
Here, the one who is begging is the *ālambana* (the objective basis);
the praise uttered by him is the *uddīpaka* (the intensifier).
The bestowal of armor and so forth, as well as the perception of lightness and the like therein, constitute the *anubhāvas*.

The pride (*garva*) evoked by the *dhvani* in which the expressed meaning is transmuted into another sense—signified by the word "me"—and the recollection of being born of a father who is superhuman and extraordinary, are the transitory emotions (*saṃcāribhāvas*).
Furthermore, the poetic style (*vṛtti*) here, characterized by rises and pauses corresponding to each respective meaning, produces a singular aesthetic wonder for those with refined sensibilities.

For instance: in the first half [of the verse], there is a description of lightness in the donning of armor and earrings to nourish enthusiasm (*utsāha*), characterized by loose bonds suitable for that purpose;
in the second half, however, it is *uddhata* (exalted) from the outset to nourish the pride and enthusiasm residing in the speaker prior to the *mauli* (head-ornament).
Following that, in order to manifest humility in the Brahmin and to suggest the absence of pride which is its root, it is again *śithila* (loose).
For this very reason, it was said, "I inform," but not "I give" or "I bestow.
However, this [which follows] should not be cited as an example:

Hearing from the mouths of the throngs of celestial bards gathered upon the circle of the earth the fame of his unbridled, day-and-night flow of gifts to supplicants, the hair on the bodies of the gods—
thrilled with envy— stood erect, and as it quivered, milk flowed from their udders.
With showers of nectar, the celestial cow of the Lord of Gods acts like a rain-cloud in the monsoon.

In this case, although the enthusiasm directed toward the wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmagavī*)— which has as its objective all the spectators gathered in the midst of Indra’s assembly, which is ignited by the descriptions of the king’s gifts emerging from the mouths of the lords of the vassals present on the circle of the earth, which is experienced through showers of nectar flowing from above, and which is further nourished by transitory emotions such as envy— is subordinate to the praise of the king, it does not serve as the basis for the designation of a *rasa*.
For this very reason, the following verse also is not an example:
“Having traversed the earth with its oceans, islands, and principal mountains, and even the entire sky with its seven regions, Hari gazed gently with a beautiful smile.”
At that moment, his hair standing on end from the eruption of supreme joy,
the chief of the asuras bowed forward and placed his crown before him;
here, the aesthetic sentiment (rasa) has the Blessed Vāmana as its objective support (ālambana) and is intensified by the glances cast upon him by the latter.
Even though it is manifested through physical effects such as horripilation and nourished by emotions such as joy, enthusiasm is also a *guṇa* (aesthetic quality).
This is because, just as in the previous case, even when it pertains to the king (rather than another), it serves to enhance the praise of that king.
By this, the example cited by Śrīvatsalāñchana—“Generosity, which culminates in the unfeigned gift of the earth sealed by the seven oceans”—is refuted;
for since that is a case of subordinated suggestion (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*), it is not to be cited in the context of *rasadhvani*.

If it is asked: "But even in the verse beginning with 'akaruṇam avakṛtya' (having mercilessly cut off...), since the suggested *dānavīra* (heroic generosity) serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the praise of Karṇa, how can it be considered *dhvani*?"—this is true;
for in this case, the poet’s intention consists merely in repeating the words of Karṇa, and thus there is an absence of intentionality regarding the praise of Karṇa itself.
Furthermore, because it is impossible for Karṇa’s self-praise to have any intended meaning given his great magnanimity, such praise is not the literal meaning of the sentence at all;
rather, it is merely inferred in its own substratum by the mark (*liṅga*) of such enthusiasm following the cognition of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*).
However, in a verse describing a king, since the intention is indeed the praise of the king, that praise constitutes the literal meaning of the sentence itself.
The second is as follows:
“O pigeon, let not even the slightest fear arising from the hawk touch you;
today I have treated this body, which is the vessel for the welfare of your life, as if it were a blade of grass.”
Alternatively, the arrangement [of the words] is as follows: “O hawk, let not even the slightest desire for the pigeon touch you;
this most beautiful body has been surrendered by me to you today.”
This is Śibi’s speech directed toward the hawk regarding the pigeon;
here, the pigeon is the *ālambana* (the objective basis),
and the resulting agitation is the *uddīpana* (the excitant).
The offering of one's own body for his sake is the *anubhāva* (the external manifestation).
Nor should it be argued that this results in the designation of the *dānavīra* (hero of generosity) due to the occasion of giving the body;
for, since the hawk and the pigeon have entered into the relationship of prey and predator, there is no petitioner for Śibi’s body, and thus no such [heroic] perception occurs.
Because the offering of the hawk’s body is expressed as an exchange, being conditioned by the protection of the pigeon’s body.
An example of the third [type] is as follows:
"Having routed the wretched gods in battle, O Ten-faced One, you carry [the goddess] away..."
"But as for you, what is this preparation of mine against your boldness of power?
Let Bhava, whose majesty has swallowed the entire web of the universe with the flames rising from his forehead,
withstand the force of the arrow discharged from my bow."
This is the speech of the Blessed Lord Rāma directed toward the Ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa).
Here, "being here" (*iha bhava*) is the objective basis (*ālambana*);
"the sight of battle" (*raṇadarśana*) is the excitant (*uddīpana*).
The transitory emotion (*saṃcārībhāva*) is pride, characterized by the power of contempt for the Ten-faced one (*Rāvaṇa*).

Here, the style (*vṛtti*) is non-exalted (*anuddhatā*), because in the context of the gods, it reveals their timidity in order to convey that they do not take the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) as their objective support.

In the section concerning the Ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa), although it is exalted for the purpose of demonstrating his heroism in subduing the pride of the gods, it does not reach excellence because, due to his contempt, the enthusiasm directed toward Rāma is not adopted as its objective; consequently, the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) based on that [enthusiasm] fails to be realized.

However, in the section concerning the Blessed Lord Bhava (Śiva), because he serves as the supreme and most excellent objective determinant (*ālambana-vibhāva*), the heroic flavor (*vīra-rasa*) based on him—which is full of vigor—is fully realized, and thus it is pre-eminently exalted.
The fourth is as follows:
“Let the fortune of sovereignty perish instantly, or let the edges of swords fall upon me;
let Death seize my head by force, but my mind shall not depart even slightly from dharma.”
This is Yudhiṣṭhira’s speech directed toward one who says, "An enemy must be conquered even by unrighteous means.
Here, the subject matter of dharma is the *ālambana* (the objective basis).
The consideration of such statements as, "One should never abandon dharma out of desire, nor out of fear, nor out of greed, even for the sake of life," constitutes the *uddīpana* (the excitant).
The acceptance of the severing of one's head and so forth is the *anubhāva* (consequent action);
fortitude (*dhṛti*) is the *saṃcārī* (transitory state).
Thus, the fourfold nature of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) has been elaborated in accordance with the views of the ancients.
In reality, however, many varieties of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) can be identified, just as there are for the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*).

For instance, in the verse beginning with "May [my body] immediately go to destruction," if the final line is rearranged to "But my mind does not depart even slightly from the truth," it becomes a different poem altogether,
because the heroic sentiment of truth (*satyavīra*) is thereby established.

Nor should it be argued that because truth (*satya*) is included within *dharma*, the heroism of truth is also subsumed under the heroic sentiment of *dharma* alone; for if that were so, since generosity (*dāna*) and compassion (*dayā*) are also included within *dharma*, it would be inappropriate to count their respective heroisms separately from the heroism of *dharma*.
In this way, the heroism of wisdom (*pāṇḍityavīra*) is also perceived.
For example:
"Even if the Lord of Speech himself, or even the presiding deity of those very words, were to speak thus:
'I am here before you, having crossed the ocean of verbal expression by means of the recollection of Hayānana.'"

In this passage, the speaker’s *utsāha* (energy) is perceived; it has as its objective support (*ālambana*) Bṛhaspati and others, is ignited by the sight of the assembly and so forth, is manifested through the experience of disregarding all learned men, and is nourished by the transitory emotion (*saṃcāribhāva*) of pride (*garva*).
Now, one might object: "Is this not the heroism of battle (*yuddhavīratva*), since 'battle-ness' is expressed here as being common to both [the heroic and the martial]? If this is argued:
What would you say to a hero of patience?
For instance:
"Even if my enemy were to continuously blow a dense mass of fire upon my head,"
"Let him strike me with the edge of a sword; I shall not speak even a single syllable.
This is the speech of one possessed of patience. What would you say to a powerful hero?
For example:
"May the preeminent serpent abandon the earth, and may even the tortoise leave it and enjoy ease;
O Puruhūta, here in the corner of my wing, I carry this entire world without weariness."
If it is argued that this speech of Garuḍa addressed to Indra is merely an expression of pride—not indeed "heroism" (utsāha)—since in the two verses beginning with "api vakti...

pariharatu dharām," only pride is present, while in the intermediate verse only steadfastness (dhṛti) is suggested, and therefore these are instances of the suggestion of a transitory emotion (bhāvadhvani) rather than the suggestion of a rasa (rasadhvani); then why, in cases such as the heroic rasa of battle and the like, should one not likewise maintain that they are merely instances of the suggestion of pride and so forth?
Or why not consider that very general suggestion of rasa (rasadhvani-sāmānya) as already accounted for by the suggestion of its transitory emotion (vyabhicāribhāva)?
If it is argued that the cognition of the permanent emotion (sthāyibhāva) is undeniable, then the same applies to the present case as well.
However, in the verse just mentioned, no enthusiasm (utsāha) is perceived.
The claim that it is perceived in instances such as *dayāvīra* (the compassionate hero) and others is merely a royal decree.
An example of the *adbhuta* (marvelous) rasa is as follows:
"Your face is the abode for the web of the moving and unmoving world."
"Beholding the depth of the sky-like [face] slipping away, my consciousness has been stolen.
This is the speech of Yaśodā when she once beheld the face of the Blessed Vāsudeva.
Herein, the "face" is the objective support (*ālambana*).
The manifestation of the entire web of the world, including all moving and non-moving beings within [the heart], is the *uddīpana* (excitant);
the loss of mental composure is the *vibhāva* (determinant),
and the resulting physical responses such as horripilation and the dilation of the eyes are the *anubhāva* (consequent).
The transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas) such as fear and the like [are present]; however,
even though the affection directed toward the son exists here, it is not perceived because of the absence of a manifesting agent (vyañjaka).
Or, even if that [beauty] were recognized, it would be inappropriate for wonder to function as a subordinate element (guṇa).
Likewise, even devotion in the form "This is some great person" cannot arise at all, because it is obstructed by the certain conviction "This is my child.
Therefore, one should not even suspect that wonder could be subordinate in that case either.
As for that which was cited by the ancient crest-jewels of connoisseurs:
"Wondrous is this great new incarnation!"
"Whence comes this radiance? This is a truly novel manner of being!

What extraordinary fortitude! Oh, what power! What an indescribable form! This is a brand-new creation!"—to this, it must be said: let wonder indeed be recognized here; however, in what way does this constitute the ground for the designation of the *adbhuta-rasa* (the marvelous sentiment) as a *dhvani* (suggestive poetry)?

Because the devotion residing in the worshipper—which is the primary element—serves as the intensifier for the specific Great Being who is the object of praise, this [devotion] is subordinate [to that subject].

This is as seen, for example, in the *Gītā* within the *Mahābhārata*, in the sequence of verses beginning with Arjuna, who has beheld the Universal Form: "I see all the gods, O God, in Your body, as well as the hosts of various beings.
In this way, its status as a *rasa-alaṃkāra* (an ornament consisting of rasa) is appropriate.
If it is argued that devotion is not perceived here at all, let the connoisseurs understand this with eyes half-closed in wonder.
An example of the comic (hāsya) is as follows:
"This novel argument has been set forth in the treatise composed by the venerable father."
"O friend, is the limb of cows not first and foremost a purifier? Or how could it be otherwise for the wife of the donkey's husband?
Here, the son of a logician (*tārkikaputra*) is the objective basis (*ālambana*);
his fearless speech is the stimulant (*uddīpikā*).

The manifestations such as the radiance of the teeth and so forth, as well as the transitory states such as agitation and so forth, are the consequents (*anubhāva*) and the transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*).
Regarding this, they say:
"It is held that there are two divisions of this [rasa]: that which resides within oneself and that which resides in another."
Abiding within the self, it arises for the seer merely through the act of observation.

Upon seeing another person laughing, a state of non-apprehension (avibhāva) arises; that which is known by the experts as the rasa of humor (hāsya-rasa) is proclaimed to be "situated in another" (parastha).
This [meditation] may belong to those who are superior, middling, or even inferior;
it is said to exist in three states, and there are six other divisions of it.
The wise declare that a smile (*smita*) and a laugh (*hasita*) occur in a superior person;
whereas a derisive laugh (*vihasita*) and a loud laugh (*upahasita*) occur in a middling man.
Below, "laughter" (*apahasita*) and "excessive laughter" (*atihasita*) are described:
[the former] with slightly blooming cheeks and with side-glances that are not intense.
A sweet smile with teeth not visible is called *smita* (a gentle smile),
provided it is characterized by a face, eyes, and cheeks that are fully blossomed.
When the teeth are slightly visible, that is considered a smile;
it is accompanied by sound, sweet, directed toward the body, and characterized by the radiance of the face.
The wise know that a smile is characterized by contracted eyes and a low tone,
accompanied by the shrugging of shoulders and the head, and a sidelong glance.
A smile with the nostrils flared is considered "derisive laughter" (upahasita);
it arises at an inappropriate time, accompanied by tears in the eyes, and causes trembling of the shoulders and hair.

Śārṅgadeva has described the laughter called *apahasita* as having a loud, harsh sound from the thick ears and eyes flooded with a stream of tears, with the sides embraced by the hands; this [type of] laughter is considered *atihasita*. Thus it is said.
An example of the Terrible (bhayānaka) is as follows:
“Beholding a hawk approaching from the expanse of the sky, its mouth and nostrils parched,
the quail— its body trembling and its eyes agitated— was indeed unable even to move.”
In this case, the hawk is the objective determinant (ālambana);
its swift flight is the excitant (uddīpana);
and the drying of the mouth and so forth are the consequents (anubhāva).
The transitory emotions (saṃcāribhāvas) include dejection and others.
An example of the loathsome (bībhatsa) is as follows: "The pus and blood of corpses whose entrails have been torn open by claws..."
"Delighted Vetāla-women smear [the faces] with fat on their mouths.
Here, the corpses are the objective basis (*ālambana*);
the tearing of entrails and so forth is the excitant (*uddīpana*).
The physical manifestations such as bristling of the hair, closing of the eyes, and so forth are the *anubhāvas*.
The transitory states (*saṃcāribhāvas*) are agitation and the like.

Now, one might object: "In the cases of love, anger, energy, fear, sorrow, wonder, and despondency previously cited, there is a clear cognition of both the objective basis (*ālambana*) and the subjective locus (*āśraya*); however, this is not the case for laughter and disgust."

If it is argued that this is because only the object itself is perceived there, and because the listener of the verse— being the locus for the relish of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)— cannot logically be the substratum for worldly laughter or disgust, [we reply:
True.
This is because the specific spectator (*draṣṭṛpuruṣa*) who is the substratum of that [sentiment] must be implied therein;
however, if he were not so implied, there would be no obstacle to the arousal of rasa in the listener, just as there is none in the case of a verse describing one's own beloved.
Thus have the rasas been briefly defined.

When these [sentiments and so forth] are predominant, they are the cause for the designation "suggestion" (*dhvani*); however, when they are subordinate, they constitute "rasa" or "ornament" (*alaṃkāra*).
Some, however, maintain: "Only when these are predominant do they possess the status of *rasa*; otherwise, they are merely ornaments.
The designation 'rasa-ornament' is like the designation 'ornament-suggestion' (*alaṃkāra-dhvani*)."
They say that this is according to the logic of the Brahmin and the ascetic;
thus, it is only in the case of the non-perceptible succession [of the moments],
whereas otherwise, there is merely the thing-in-itself.

And these are cases where the suggested meaning has an imperceptible sequence (*asaṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya*). This is because, when the manifestation of rasa occurs instantaneously for a connoisseur, even though the sequence of the reflection upon the excitants (*vibhāva*), ensuants (*anubhāva*), and transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*) exists, it is not perceived—just as the sequence of piercing a hundred lotus petals with a hundred needles is not noticed.

It is not, however, a case of "simultaneous" suggestion (*akramavyaṅgya*), for that would result in an inconsistency regarding the relationship of cause and effect between the manifestation and its causes.
Now, how is it that these alone are the *rasas*?

Because the *bhaktirasa*— which has the Blessed One as its objective support, which is manifested by physical responses such as horripilation and the shedding of tears, which is nourished by states such as joy, and which is experienced by devotees at the time of hearing the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* and other scriptures— is impossible to deny.
In this context, devotion (*bhakti*) consisting of attachment to the Blessed One is the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*).
Nor does it deserve to be included within the *śānta* (quiescent) rasa,
because attachment is opposed to detachment (*vairāgya*).

It is said: because devotion consists of attachment toward objects such as the gods, it is subsumed under the category of *bhāva* (emotional state), and thus its status as *rasa* (aesthetic flavor) is untenable.

As it is stated: "Attachment directed toward objects such as the gods, when manifested as a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*), is called *bhāva*; its semblances (*tadābhāsa*) are those brought about by impropriety."
For such is the established doctrine of the ancients.
And if that were so, then even *rati* (erotic love) directed toward a beloved woman would have the status of a *bhāva*, since there is no difference in its nature as *rati*.

Or it might be argued: "Let it be that devotion to the Blessed One alone possesses the status of a *sthāyin* (permanent emotion), while the pleasures of love for a woman and so forth possess the status of *bhāvas* (transitory emotions), as there is no decisive evidence [to the contrary].
This, however, must be rejected, because the words of sages such as Bharata themselves possess the authority to establish the distinction between what constitutes *rasa* and what constitutes *bhāva*.
Otherwise, why would even the pleasure (*rati*) directed toward objects such as one's son not be considered a permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*)?

Or, conversely, why would emotions such as disgust (*jugupsā*) and sorrow (*śoka*) not be considered pure emotions (*śuddhabhāva*)? Thus, the entire system of aesthetics would fall into confusion, and the enumeration of nine rasas, which was constrained by the words of the Sage (Vyāsa), would be violated.
Thus, according to the scriptures alone, this is superior;
there is no mutual contradiction among these [rasas].
Among them, regarding the heroic (*vīra*) and the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*):
Of the erotic and the comic; of the heroic and the marvelous; of the heroic and the furious.
There is no contradiction between the erotic and the marvelous;
nor between the erotic and the loathsome, the erotic and the pathetic,
or the heroic and the fearful.
There is a contradiction between the peaceful (*śānta*) and the fierce (*raudra*), as well as between the peaceful and the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*).
In this regard, a poet who desires to nourish the primary sentiment (*prakṛtarasa*) must not compose elements of a conflicting sentiment within the poem that manifests it.
For if that [other rasa] were manifested while it exists, it would subvert the primary one;
or else, by the maxim of Sundopasunda, there would be a destruction of both.
However, if the coexistence of even two conflicting rasas in a single place is desired, then the conflict must be resolved through a prescribed method.
To explain: opposition (*virodha*) is first of two kinds—opposition of coexistence and opposition of cognition.
The former consists in the absence [of one thing] from the locus of the other.
The second [type of contradiction] is characterized by the fact that one cognition is dependent upon another cognition of that same object.
In that case, when a contradictory element is established in a different locus, the first [contradiction] is removed;

for example, when the heroic sentiment (*vīra-rasa*) is to be described as residing in the hero (*nāyaka*), the presence of the terrifying (*bhayānaka*) sentiment in the antagonist (*pratināyaka*) is removed.

In this context, by the term "rasa" (flavor), its limiting adjunct—the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*)—is intended. This is because rasa resides in the spectator (*sāmājika*), not in the hero (*nāyaka*) and others; furthermore, since it consists of non-dual bliss, no contradiction is possible.
The example:
"In your presence, with your staff-like arms wielding the drawn bow,
enemies did not stand their ground at all, like deer before a lion."
When a second rasa, which is not incompatible with the first, remains in the interval like a mediator between two parties, the first rasa also subsides.

For example, in the narrative (*ākhyāyikā*) composed by me, when the description of the great sage Śvetaketu—residing in the hermitage of Kaṇva—is set forth as being dominated by the *śānta* (peaceful) rasa, the description of his passion for the beautiful maiden proceeds by interposing the *adbhuta* (wonderful) rasa, as in: "What is this unprecedented form?
What is this ineffable sweetness of the arrangement of words? By thus establishing the wonderful in the interval, the [initial] state is suspended.
Or as it is said:
"Heroes traveling in celestial chariots through the sky, embraced by divine damsels,
behold their own bodies surrounded by female jackals."

In this verse, between the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the loathsome (*bībhatsa*), which have respectively the celestial nymphs and the immortal body as their objective supports, the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*)—implied by the attainment of heaven—is interposed.
This "interposition" consists in the fact that its aesthetic relish occurs at a time situated within the interval between the relishes of those two.

And this is quite clear in the present verse: for the relish of the heroic occurs immediately after the relish of the erotic in the first half, and the relish of the loathsome follows immediately after in the second half.

Regarding the series of verses beginning with "bhūreṇudigdhān" from the *Kāvyaprakāśa*: due to the force of the aesthetic materials (*sāmagrī*) of the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) rasa first perceived, there occurs first the relish (*carvaṇā*) of the loathsome; subsequently, when there is the relish of the heroic (*vīra*) rasa—whose materials include the fearless abandonment of life and so forth, which are projected by those same [loathsome] materials—that is the relish of the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*).

This is the distinction. Thus, by means of the relish of the indifferent [element], once the obstructing cognition has ceased, the emergence of the relish of the obstructed [element] occurs without impediment; this is the established meaning.
There is no contradiction between the subordinate and the principal, whether the principal is one thing and the two subordinates are another, or both subordinates belong to the same principal.
Because it would follow that the status of being a subordinate member [of a compound] is untenable—
just as in the verse:
"She was met with courtesy by her friends, who were suddenly filled with smiles, those impassioned glances which are the ministers of Love."
O young girl, why do you not today show me even the slightest bit of respect with your charming arrangements of words? Alas! Tell me.
This is the speech of the hero directed toward his heroine who has fallen down before him and passed away.

Here, the love residing in the hero— manifested through the objective basis (ālambana) of the heroine, the consequents (anubhāvas) such as the shedding of tears, and the transitory states (saṃcāribhāvas) such as agitation and despondency— is the predominant element because it is the subject at hand, being revealed by a complete set of causes (sāmagrī) that are common to both [the hero and the heroine].
Thus, because it intensifies the sorrow (*śoka*), [the emotion] is an auxiliary (*aṅga*).

However, if the love (*rati*) residing in the hero is not perceived here, but rather—due to the aforementioned collection of factors and because of the context—it is understood as sorrow alone, then it is indeed the love residing in the heroine that is intended; this love has the hero as its objective support (*ālambana*), is manifested by acts such as going out to meet him, and is nourished by emotions such as joy.
In this regard, let it be a subordinate element (*aṅga*), because it is universally accepted that the heroine's love serves as the cause for intensifying the hero's grief.
Nor should it be argued: "How can it be a subordinate element if, due to the heroine's destruction, the love residing in her is no longer present?"
Since proximity (*saṃnidhāna*) is not a restrictive factor for being a constituent part (*aṅga*), it is logical that what is remembered as such should indeed possess the status of a constituent part.
As in the case of two constituent parts—for example:
"The [hands] raised toward the mass of her braided hair..."
The side-glances of the fair-browed wives of your rival kings—
curved toward both sides, cast down with anger, and avoided from afar by the hem of their garments—
are now being seized with haste.
"Among the trees moving through the thickets, which ones are not covered in thorns?

Here, through the two components of the *samāsokti* (condensed expression)—namely, the apprehension of the trees and the lovers as the agents of the actions of "moving" and "being covered in thorns"—the manifested sentiments of *karuṇa* (pathos) and *śṛṅgāra* (erotic love) serve as subordinate elements (*aṅga*) to the dominant emotion (*bhāva*) of devotion toward the king.
Furthermore, one who desires the full nourishment of the primary sentiment must certainly include even a conflicting sentiment by making it subordinate (*bādhyatvena*).
For when this is the case, a certain splendor arises for the subject described by the conqueror of enemies;

and the subordination (*bādhyatva*) of a rasa consists in the obstruction of its own development, even though its own constituent factors (*svāṅga*) are present, due to the powerful limbs of a conflicting rasa.
However, the subordination of a transitory emotion (*vyabhicārin*) results merely from the obstruction of the development of the rasa to which it belongs.
But it is not [non-manifestation] due to a lack of manifestation,
because there is no sublation regarding manifestation.
Nor should it be said that there is no manifestation because of an obstruction caused by the manifestation of a contradictory factor.
Because at the time of the cognition of the word and meaning that manifest that [aesthetic flavor], there is no presence of the cognition of the word and meaning that manifest the opposing factor;

because there is no evidence for postulating a relationship of mutual obstruction between them; and because it would entail the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of the variegation of mental states (bhāva-śabalatā).

Since the obstruction to the production of rasa is established by experience, it is logical that the powerful factors of contradiction (virodhy-aṅgas) act as obstructions specifically with respect to that [production].
Furthermore, even in cases where there is the manifestation of two contradictory elements through the power of a common attribute (sādhāraṇa-viśeṣaṇa), the contradiction is set aside;
for example: [Example omitted per instructions]
"Utterly intoxicated by youth and deeply enamored in the great battle,
O hero, those enemies lie there embracing the earth.
Even when a rasa is thus composed through the establishment of non-contradiction, it is not proper to designate it by the word "rasa" or by words such as "śṛṅgāra" (the erotic).

Because that would result in the rasa being something not to be tasted (*anāsvādya*), and because it has been stated that its tasting is accomplished solely through the *vyañjana* (suggestive function).
If it is asked: "What fault is there in a case where the rasa, manifested by the *vibhāvas* and so forth, is denoted by its own word? [the answer follows].
For, in the case of making the suggested sense (vyaṅgya) the expressed (vācya), the general defect known as *vamana* will be mentioned later;

furthermore, because it fails to produce cognition in the form that delimits aesthetic relish (*āsvādyatāvacchedaka*), the function of the expressed meaning in the context of rasa is like the behavior of a monkey, and thus constitutes a specific defect.
Likewise, the verbal expression of the permanent moods (*sthāyin*) and the transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*) is also a defect.

Thus, when there is an incorrect apprehension or a delayed apprehension of the *vibhāvas* (determinants) and *anubhāvas* (consequents), there is no relish of rasa; therefore, these constitute defects.

Furthermore, the composition of subordinate elements (*aṅgas*) belonging to a rasa that is either of equal or greater strength and contrary to the primary rasa obstructs the nourishment of the primary rasa, and is thus a defect.

In a literary work (*prabandha*), if the primary rasa is interrupted by another incidental topic and then rekindled, the audience does not experience the relish of rasa with full intensity; this is the defect known as "interrupted rekindling" (*vicchinnadīpana*).
Likewise, there is the introduction of this or that rasa at an occasion unsuitable for its introduction, and its interruption at an occasion where it ought not to be interrupted;

for example, when the description of dharma— such as the twilight worship and the sacrifice to the gods— is underway, there is the description of the passion between a certain lover and a certain beloved woman.

Just as it would be improper for a leader to describe his twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*) and so forth while his enemies—fierce in the heat of a great battle and standing before him—are uttering words that pierce the vital organs;
likewise, one should not describe the various deeds or the manifold riches of a subordinate character such as an antagonist as being superior to those belonging to the hero.
For if they were, the intended excellence of the hero would fail to be established.
Furthermore, the nourishment of the aesthetic flavor (*rasapoṣa*) resulting from that [description] would not occur.

Nor should it be argued that the excellence of the antagonist (*pratināyaka*) must not be described because it serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) for the excellence of the hero (*nāyaka*), who overcomes him;
for we accept the description of such excellence of the antagonist as is conducive to accomplishing the excellence of the hero who overcomes him.
This is because only that which is opposed to it can be negated.

Nor should it be argued that the excellence of the counter-position— even when described in relation to the subject under discussion— would surpass the excellence residing in the subject merely by destroying its own locus,
and therefore it does not constitute a fault.
For if this were the case, O Great King, there would be no excellence whatsoever for the hero at hand—just like that wretched Śabara who killed someone merely by discharging a poisoned arrow.
Likewise, if the connection between the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), its objective basis (*ālambana*), and its substratum (*āśraya*) were not maintained from time to time, it would be a defect;
for the stream of the perception of *rasa* is dependent upon that connection, and in the absence of such connection, it would cease.
Likewise, the description of an object that does not assist the intended rasa is indeed a defect, because it causes a lack of interest in the primary rasa.
However, impropriety (*anaucitya*) must be avoided because it is a cause for the disruption of the rasa;
and this disruption is like the stinging sensation caused by the falling of grit into a beverage or similar drink.

And that [distinction] consists in the difference between whatever appropriate substance, quality, action, and so forth is established for each member of that manifold world—such as caste, place, time, color, stage of life, age, condition, temperament, and social conduct—by either worldly convention or the scriptures.

For example, what is inappropriate for caste and the rest is as follows: qualities such as valor, strength, and prowess in cattle and the like; and qualities such as gentleness and the like in lions and the like.
In heaven, there is old age, disease, and so forth; on the earthly realm, there is the consumption of nectar and so forth;
in the cold season, there is sporting in the water and so forth.
In summer, one should attend to the fire;
hunting is for the Brāhmaṇa,
and receiving gifts is for the Bāhuja (Kṣatriya).
The study of the Vedas by a Śūdra;
the chewing of betel-leaf by a religious student (brahmacārin) and an ascetic (yati); and the taking of a wife [by such persons].
The pursuit of women by the young and the old, the lack of passion in the youth,
and the behavior of the wealthy among the poor.
The wealthy may adopt the conduct of the poor;
the constituent elements (prakṛtis) are divine, non-divine, and both divine and non-divine.

The [heroic characters] are the *dhīrodātta*, *dhīroddhata*, *dhīralalita*, and *dhīraśānta*, who are characterized primarily by enthusiasm, anger, passion, delight, and world-weariness, and are classified as superior, middling, or inferior. In this regard, although the stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*) such as love and so forth are equal in all cases, the description of all the attendant emotional states (*anubhāva*) must be made explicit for divine beings—just as it is for humans—in the case of love in its form of sexual union; and likewise, the description of anger, which is capable of reducing the world to ashes and performs many wonders such as the overturning of day and night, must be made explicit for non-divine beings—just as it is for divine ones.
For, upon the cognition of the object's adorability and the cognition of the actor's falsity, there would result the failure of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) to arise.
Nor should it be argued that the knowledge of adorability does not arise because of the process of universalization (*sādhāraṇīkaraṇa*);
for the hypothesis of universalization is postulated only in those cases where the arousal of *rasa* among sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*) is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Otherwise, even when describing the passion of one's own father toward his own mother, there would result the awakening of rasa in a sensitive reader (*sahṛdaya*). However, Jayadeva and others, in their compositions such as the *Gītagovinda*, have shattered this convention—agreed upon by all sensitive readers—as if with elephants intoxicated by rut; and it is now appropriate for contemporary [writers] to describe in that manner, following their example.

Likewise, one should not address those who are inferior to oneself by means of speech accompanied by great respect on account of their own superior learning, age, caste, stage of life (*āśrama*), or austerity;
rather, one should so address those who are superior to oneself even when they are inferior.

Furthermore, in that regard, such forms of address as "Venerable Sir" (*tatrabhavan*) or "Blessed One" (*bhagavan*) are to be used only for sages, teachers, deities, and the like, and not for kings and others.
Only by the most excellent twice-born, not by the low-born such as Śūdras and others;
and only by addressing him with titles such as "Supreme Lord" (Parameśvara) and so forth, [is he worshipped] as a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Sages and others such as they are not to be instructed;
thus they have said:
"There is no cause for the disruption of aesthetic flavor (rasa) other than impropriety."
"But the composition of established propriety is the supreme secret of rasa.
To the extent that there is nourishment of rasa through even what is improper, that is not prevented, because only that which is antagonistic to rasa is to be prohibited. Therefore—
“O Brahmin, this is not the time for study; stand silently outside. Speak but little, O Bṛhaspati of dull wit; this is not the assembly of the Wielder of the Thunderbolt.”
"Cease your lute, Nārada! Enough with these songs of praise and conversation, Tumburu! The Lord of Laṅkā, whose heart is shattered by the arrows of Sītā’s longing, is not yet composed.

In this verse from a certain drama, there is an impropriety in the words of the doorkeeper—who, while intended to nourish the supreme sovereignty that serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) within the context of the sentiment of love-in-separation (*vipralambhaśṛṅgāra*)—since those words consist of insults directed at Brahmā and the other gods.
There is no fault;

for in the same way, even in such speech of the Vidūṣaka as "O Ale! O Le! having produced a sound, having deceived with a necklace made of knots of green grass-tips, the Brāhmaṇas have performed the rite of bestowing wealth upon fools," the use of the word *re* and so forth is appropriate because it accords with the comic effect.

This direction has indeed been shown; by means of it, the wise may infer other matters as well. And regarding these flavors (rasas) that have been described, they speak of three qualities (guṇas) known as sweetness (mādhurya), vigor (ojas), and clarity (prasāda).

In that regard, the sweetness found in the erotic sentiment known as union is surpassed in the pathetic; it is surpassed by that [pathetic] in the erotic of separation; and it is surpassed even by those in the tranquil.
"Because it generates a progressively more intense flow of mental activity (*cittadruti*),
[rasa] is superior in *karuṇa* and *śānta* compared to *saṃyoga-śṛṅgāra*, and in *vipralambha* compared to those two as well"— so say some others.

Others, however, maintain that while there is indeed a progressive intensification from *saṃyoga-śṛṅgāra* through *karuṇa*, *vipralambha*, and *śānta*, there is no further gradation within those [latter three].
In that regard, the sūtra of the predecessors— “It [sweetness] is possessed of excellence in Karuṇa, Vipralambha, and its [Karuna’s] Śānta”— is favorable to the first and last views,
because two interpretations are possible depending on whether the word *krameṇa* (in sequence), which occurs in the subsequent sūtra, is applied or not applied to it.

However, regarding the middle view, if there is the experience of connoisseurs as a witness for the fact that *Vipralambha* possesses a greater degree of sweetness than *Karuṇa* and *Śānta*, then that experience is authoritative.
In the heroic (*vīra*), the loathsome (*bībhatsa*), and the furious (*raudra*) rasas, there is a progressive intensification of vigor (*ojas*),
because they generate a mental radiance that increases more and more.
Some maintain that the marvelous (*adbhuta*), the comic (*hāsya*), and the terrifying (*bhayānaka*) possess a combination of two qualities.
Others, however, maintain that it is merely clarity (*prasāda*).
Clarity, moreover, is common to all sentiments (*rasas*) and all compositions.
Furthermore, these qualities (*guṇas*) should be employed in succession through three mental states known as melting (*druti*), brilliance (*dīpti*), and expansion (*vikāsa*).
That is to say, they are produced by the relishing (*carvaṇā*) of flavors qualified by those respective qualities.
Thus, when these qualities— which are properties of rasa alone— have been determined, there is "sweet composition" (*madhurā racanā*).

Mammaṭabhaṭṭa and others maintain that conventional expressions such as "the *bandha* (composition) is *ojasvī* (vigorous)" are merely figurative (*aupacārika*), just like the expression "this man is a hero" (*śūra*).

As for those qualities—sweetness (*mādhurya*), vigor (*ojas*), and clarity (*prasāda*)—which have been described as belonging exclusively to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), what is the proof for their being properties of *rasa*?
If it is argued that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself is the proof, we say no.

If it is argued that—just as there is an experience of the hot touch residing in fire as distinct from its effects such as burning—there is likewise no experience of qualities residing in rasa as distinct from the mental states (cittavṛtti) such as melting (*druti*), which are the effects of rasa;

and that therefore, since rasas characterized by such qualities are the causes of melting and so forth, those qualities are inferred by virtue of being the delimiters of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*)—we reply:
since the causality of rasas is established through their own specific individual forms alone, it is more cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate [additional] qualities.

It should not be said that the state of being a cause for melting (*druti*) through the possession of sweetness (*mādhuryavatva*) in the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), pathetic (*karuṇa*), and peaceful (*śānta*) sentiments is simpler than the postulation of causality in their individual forms; for,

since the opponent accepts that qualities such as "sweeter" (*madhurataratva*) and so forth serve as the causes for a gradation of effects such as "more intense melting" (*drutatara*), the causality based on the mere possession of sweetness becomes redundant (*gaḍubhūta*).
And thus, there is parsimony (lāghava) in [accepting] causality precisely in its specific form.

Furthermore, since the self is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), it is untenable for sweetness and other such qualities to have the nature of being qualities of the self's own form or taste. Likewise, it is also untenable for them to have the nature of being qualities such as love (rati) that belong to the self's limiting adjunct (upādhi).
Because there is an absence of evidence, and because, according to the system of others, it is improper for one quality to possess another quality.
If it is asked, "How then is there the conventional usage such as 'the erotic sentiment is sweet'? [the answer follows].

In that case, let sweetness (*mādhurya*) and so forth be either the cause of mental states such as melting (*druti*) and the like, or simply melting and the like themselves, by way of the relation of being a cause.
As for conventional usage, it remains unimpaired, just like the usage "the smell of a horse is hot" (*vājigandha-uṣṇa*).

Furthermore, the state of being a "prompter" (prayojakatva) must be understood as something distinct from the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth, and as residing precisely within the arrangement of words, meanings, and aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*).
Consequently, there is no over-extension of the term in common usage.

Likewise, since such qualities as sweetness (*mādhurya*) and the like exist in both words and meanings, those like me maintain that metaphorical treatment (*upacāra*) is not at all to be postulated here.
The ancients,
however, [state]: "Cohesion (śleṣa), clarity (prasāda), evenness (samatā), sweetness (mādhurya), softness (sukumāratā),
explicitness of meaning (arthavyakti), loftiness (udāratva), vigor (ojas), beauty (kānti), and composure (samādhi)."
Thus they declare ten qualities of sound and likewise ten qualities of meaning;
the names, moreover, are those very same ones.
But the definition is distinct. For instance:

*śleṣa* (punning conjunction), which is synonymous with "compactness" (*gāḍhatva*), is a particular arrangement of phonemes of a single type through their combination (*saṃhitā*), which serves as the cause for the appearance of unity even among words that are otherwise distinct.
As they say: "Cohesion (*śliṣṭa*) is the absence of looseness (*aspaṣṭaśaithilya*).
For example: "The five-faced lion [of the king], who is adept at routing the surging flood of the intense pride of the elephants—the poverty that attacks the trees of the learned without ceasing.
*Prasāda* (clarity) of composition is the blending of compactness and looseness in a non-sequential manner.
For example:
"How can we, these few, describe your heroism,
O Indra upon earth..."
O you whose brows are curved in play and whose eyes are ruddy, as you gaze upon the circle of your arms,

the trees growing from the ground within the cave-dwellings of the Vindhya forest were illuminated at that moment by the thousands of rays emitted from your ornaments, which were jagged with the brilliance of rows of rubies.

In this context, it should be understood that everything up to "yasmin" indicates looseness, that which ends with the word "bhru" indicates firmness, and again, that which ends with "nayanā" indicates the first [stage], and so forth.
Uniformity (*samatā*) is the absence of deviation from the style from the commencement until the conclusion.
As will be illustrated in the forthcoming examples of sweetness (*mādhurya*):
in those cases, both the opening and the conclusion are composed exclusively in the *upanāgarikā* style.
Sweetness consists in the state of having separate words (*pṛthakpadatva*), provided that it is composed of phonemes other than short vowels followed by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*).
For example:
"A garland of lotuses is exceedingly harsh, while lotus stalks are not delicate enough for comparison;
if such is the tenderness of your limbs, then what talk can there be of young shoots?"
Sukumāratā (smoothness) is the state of being composed of non-harsh syllables.
For example:

"The lovely state of the intoxicating-eyed woman— worthy of veneration with her ear-ornaments swaying upon the contours of her cheeks, which are marked by thick drops of perspiration— sprouts joy in my mind through mere remembrance."
In this case, there is [the quality of] *ojaḥ* in the first half, while in the second half there is also *mādhurya*.
*Arthavyakti* (clarity of meaning) consists in the fact that the connection of the meanings is perceived instantaneously (*jhagiti*).
As in the verse beginning with "nitarām," *audāratā* (loftiness) is characterized by a ruggedness consisting in the arrangement of hard-sounding phonemes.
For example:

"When Vināyaka was providing amusement by means of a series of rhythmic claps offered by the Pramathas, who were swollen with the weight of their joy, and while the sound of his hand-drum and kettledrums resounded..."
"The dancer, stripped of his garment, dances with the forceful mass of his matted hair raised aloft, while the spray from his freshly split frontal-forehead [third eye] bursts forth.
Regarding this, the commentators on the *Kāvyaprakāśa* explain that "the quality of the words being as if dancing constitutes *vikaṭatā* (strangeness)."
And they cite such examples as: "The anklets of the dancers, fixed upon their own feet, suddenly rang out," and so forth.
In that regard, how the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* is consistent in subsuming such a form of *udāratā*—characterized by grandiosity—within *ojas*, only those [authorities] themselves know.
For in this case, there is no flash of brilliance (*pratibhāna*) due to the abundance of *ojas*.

In the verse beginning with "viniviṣṭair nūpurair narta-," although there is a trace of *ojas*, it does not produce aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*). Furthermore, connoisseurs do not perceive a quality of "being as if dancing" in the phonemes (*varṇa*) therein.
In another portion, however, there is sweetness alone;
while *ojas* consists of intensity characterized by an abundance of short vowels followed by conjunct consonants.
For example:

"She, who utterly eclipses the pride of the beautiful circles of waves of the milk-ocean as it is churned by Mount Mandara— which is being whirled about, pulled by the hands of the rows of gods and demons possessed of ego— "
"O ornament of the earth, your glories, beheld with joy by throngs of ascetics languid from the exhaustion of thirst, adorn the entire expanse of the world.
Or, as in the previously cited example beginning with "May this [man] fall mercilessly," and so forth.
*Kānti* (elegance) is the extraordinary brilliance consisting of beauty found in words employed by avoiding those words suitable for the usage of unrefined Vaidikas and others.
As in the previously cited example beginning with "nitarām" (exceedingly),
the successive establishment of intensity and laxity [of the mind] is *samādhi*.
Regarding these two alone, the ancient masters have employed the designations "ascent" (āroha) and "descent" (avaroha);
for it is their very sequence that distinguishes them,
since they occur there in a reversed order.
For example:
"The lotus-face of him whose speech— releasing nothing but nectar— is the companion of the lofty and shimmering waves of the Ganges as it flows unimpeded from heaven."
In this verse, there is an ascent (*āroha*) in the first half-verse,
whereas in the third quarter-verse there is a descent (*avaroha*).
Although the letters that suggest sweetness (*mādhurya*) are present in the word "Gaṅgā" and so forth, because they fall within a long compound, that sweetness does not reach full development.
In the latter half [of the verse], that too [is included].
These ten are the qualities of sound (*śabda-guṇa*).

Thus, through a succession of actions, the connection (*saṃsarga*)—in the form of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—between the clever action, its lack of clarity, and the reasoning that establishes it, constitutes *śleṣa* (punning concatenation).
Lucidity (*prasāda*) is the clarity of meaning, consisting in the quality of having a single word for each intended sense.
For example: "Her face indeed resembles a lotus," and so forth.
A counter-example, however, is: "A face that imitates the beauty of a lotus," and so forth.
*Samatā* (evenness) consists in the construction of meaning without a break in the established style (*prakrama*).
As it is said:
"Hari is my father, Hari is my mother, Hari is my brother, Hari is my friend;
I see Hari everywhere; nothing other than Hari appears to me."
In this regard, the creation [of the verse] beginning with "Viṣṇu is the brother" and so forth involves the defect of *vaiṣamya* (unevenness), which consists in a break in the established sequence;
whereas *mādhurya* (sweetness) consists in the variety of expression (*uktivaicitrya*), which is the restatement of a single utterance through a different stylistic turn.
For example:
"Let Brahmā perform his meditation without hesitation or limit; oh, let Hari sleep happily upon Śeṣa; let Hara dance incessantly."
"Enough with expiations, and likewise with austerities, gifts, and sacrifices,
if you, the mother of all desires, remain awake in this world.

Here, the point— that there is no purpose whatsoever for injunctions and the like— is expressed through a variety of phrasing in the form of an exhortation to practice meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and so forth.
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of it not being renewed; gentleness (*sukumāratā*) consists in the absence of harshness, which is the state of not causing grief at an inappropriate time.
For example: "This traveler, distressed by separation from his beloved, goes with haste.
However, in the case of "distressed by the death of his beloved," there is harshness (*pāruṣya*) because of the presence of the word "death" (*maraṇa*), which conveys grief.
And this is subsumed under the fault of indecorum (*aślīlatā*).
*Arthavyakti* (manifestation of meaning) is the description of both the unique action and form of an object that is to be described.
For example:
"In the midst of the elders, the lotus-eyed lady restrained me— who was desiring to strike the lotus-eyed one—
with her tongue held fast by her teeth and her eyes trembling."
This very same [quality] is now designated by contemporary [theorists] as the figure of speech *svabhāvokti* (description of nature).
Nobility (*udāratā*) consists in the avoidance of vulgar meanings, such as in the verse: "O wife, give me a kiss for the satisfaction of my fierce lust."
The expression of a single referent by many words, and of many [referents] by one;
likewise, the expression of a single sentence-meaning by many sentences.
Ojas is fivefold: the expression of the meaning of many sentences by means of a single sentence, and the presence of intentional significance in qualifiers.
As they say:

"The composition of a sentence regarding the meaning of a word, and the expression of words regarding the meaning of a sentence; expansion and contraction, and its possession of intended significance—this is called *prauḍhi* (mature artistry)."

The meaning is that *oja* (vigorousness) is fivefold: the four modes of *prauḍhi* (maturity), which consist of the two things to be established in the first half [of the verse]—namely, elaboration (*vyāsa*) and brevity (*samāsa*)—plus intentionality (*sābhiprāyatva*).
*Prauḍhi* is the variety of expression.
As it is said:
"At the time when the splendor of the friend of the lotus grove begins to manifest, [the moon] quickly goes to its destruction in the kingdom of the Lord of Night."
"And there appeared the diversion of men emerging from the mouth of the Supreme Person, their voices as sweet as honey.
Here, the first quarter-verse is intended to express the single meaning of the word *uṣas*.
This should be understood as applying to what follows as well:
"The rays of the sun shine, having adorned the entire horizon and acting as skilled collyrium for the clusters of lotus-eyes of the women who have been separated [from their lovers]."

In this context, the term *khaṇḍitā* (a woman whose lover has been unfaithful) is used to denote the meaning of the sentence: "The husband of whom [returns] to his house in the morning from the home of another woman. And: "Fate, unrestrained among men, gives happiness when not asked for, yet does not give when asked; it even takes away everything."

In this regard, while the intended meaning of the sentence is that "everything is dependent on destiny," there is an extensive elaboration (*vistara*) consisting of various sentence constructions expressed by the term *vyāsa*:
"Having learned the meaning of the Vedas from the mouth of the sage performing austerities, he,
with his soul fixed upon Vāsudeva..."
He entered the supreme state.
Here, [it is said that] "the sage was performing austerities" and "he mastered the meaning of the Vedas from his mouth."

“Immediately thereafter, he caused his mind to enter Vāsudeva, the Supreme Brahman,” and “thereupon he became liberated”— this collection of sentence-meanings is unified into a single syntactical meaning through the relationship of the subject and the predicate by means of the present participle (*śatṛ*), the absolutive suffix (*ktvā*), the *bahuvrīhi* compound, and the finite verb (*tiṅanta*).
Furthermore, its "intentionality" (*sābhiprāyatvam*) consists in its capacity to nourish the contextual theme.
As it is said:
"O Embodiment of Compassion, surely I too, sinking in the desert pit of worldly existence, should not be entirely neglected by You, who have rescued even Gaṇikā, Jābāli, and others."
In this context, the absence of equanimity (*upekṣā*) is nourished by the embodiment of compassion (*karuṇāmūrtitva*).
Since compassion is absent in the case of the most wicked, the words "prostitute" (*gaṇikā*) and so forth, as well as "suffering" (*sīdann*), are used to bring it about in the present instance.
Radiance (*kānti*) is the state of having an intense aesthetic flavor (*dīptarasa*).
And that state of having rasa clearly manifested is already illustrated in the section on rasa,
and will be further described there as well.
Samādhi is the poet’s contemplation as to whether this matter has not been described before, or whether it possesses the same shadow as what was previously described.
Because knowledge is established in the object through the relation of objective content (*viṣayatā*), it is a quality of the object.
Regarding this, they say that the first type— as in the verse beginning with "In search of his son Maināka"— is rare, whereas the second type occurs almost everywhere.

Others, however, regarding some of these qualities as already included within the three previously mentioned qualities and others as being either merely varieties of stylistic charm (*vaicitrya*) or even defects in certain instances— considering them redundant through the absence of faults and the presence of ornaments to be described hereafter— do not accept that many of them as independent qualities.
For instance, *śleṣa* (conciseness), *audārya* (magnificence), *prasāda* (lucidity), and *samādhi* (evenness) are included within a composition that manifests *ojas* (forcefulness).
Granted that *śleṣa* (conjunction) and *udāratā* (loftiness), which consist essentially of firm construction, may indeed be included within the arrangement (*ghaṭanā*) that manifests *ojas* (force);

however, it must be stated where *prasāda* (transparency) and *samādhi* (evenness), which consist respectively of firm and loose construction, are included— since while they may be partially included within that which manifests *ojas*, they must be included in some other part.
This is because it is easy to say that [the quality] either manifests sweetness (*mādhurya*) or manifests clarity (*prasāda*).
Furthermore, what others consider to be sweetness is precisely what we accept as a manifester of sweetness.
Thus, in all cases, the use of the term "manifested" (*vyaṅgya*) for the manifester (*vyañjaka*) is figurative.
Uniformity, however, is entirely inappropriate [in this context],
because within a single verse, a distinction between styles (mārgabheda) is desired based on whether the expression directed toward the subject matter is prominent or not.
As, for example:
“If you are truly an expert in poetic composition— speech that is exalted by its abandonment of the pride of the honey-sweetness of grapes when they are over-ripe and melting—
then, my friend, speak your poem freely in the presence of those like me;
otherwise, do not let it remain outside your heart as if it were a misdeed committed by yourself.”

In this instance, the very disparity—that the path which establishes the supramundane emanation in the third quarter of the first half-verse is not the same path that establishes the wretched poetry in the fourth quarter—is indeed a merit.

By the abandonment of vulgarity (*grāmyatva*) and harshness (*kaṣṭatva*), the qualities of loveliness (*kānti*) and softness (*saukumārya*) are already implied; and by clarity (*prasāda*), the manifestation of meaning (*arthavyakti*) is likewise attained.

Regarding the qualities of meaning (*arthaguṇa*) as well: *śleṣa* (cohesion), the four varieties beginning with *ojas* (vigour), and *uktivaicitryamātra* (mere variety of expression) do not deserve to be included among the [ten] *guṇas*, because otherwise, due to the distinctness of the variety of meaning in every verse, it would follow that there must be a different *guṇa* for each. *Prasāda* (transparency), which consists in the absence of superfluous words, [is also not a *guṇa*].
Sweetness has the form of variety in expression;
gentleness has the body of non-roughness;
and nobility has the nature of being free from vulgarity.
Equanimity (*samatā*), characterized by the absence of unevenness,
is the fifth type of *ojas*, consisting of intentional meaning;
and clarity of meaning (*arthavyakti*), consisting of the manifestation of intrinsic nature.
And *kānti* (lucidity), which consists of the manifestation of rasa,

is already implied by the elimination of defects such as *adhikapada* (redundancy), *anavīkṛtatva* (lack of freshness), *amaṅgalarūpa-āślīlatva* (indecency consisting of inauspiciousness), *grāmya* (vulgarity), *bhagnaprakrama* (break in symmetry), and *apuṣṭārtha* (insignificant meaning), as well as by the inclusion of the figure *svabhāvokti* (natural description), *rasadhvani* (suggestion of rasa), and the figure *rasavat*. Thus, these [qualities] have already been accounted for.
However, Mammaṭabhaṭṭa and others maintain that *samādhi* residing in the poet is a cause of poetry, not a quality (*guṇa*),
because if it were, then *pratibhā* (creative intuition) would also have to be considered a quality of poetry;
therefore, there are only three qualities.

In that [composition], it is adorned by the first and third letters of the consonant classes excluding the *ṭa*-class, joined with the semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*) and embellished by *anusvāra*, *parasavarṇa*, and pure nasalized sounds (*śuddhānunāsika*) employed in close proximity; and it is untouched by conjunct consonants and other such features generally or specifically prohibited as will be described hereafter.
The absence of repetition or a soft repetition consisting of the sequential arrangement [of sounds] is the manifester of *mādhurya* (sweetness).
However, the second and fourth letters of the classes (*vargyas*) are neither favorable nor unfavorable to this quality.
If they are arranged at a distance, they become agreeable even when they are discordant in close proximity,
provided that the alliteration (*anuprāsa*) does not depend upon that [close proximity].
Others, however, state that all five classes [of consonants] without distinction suggest sweetness (*mādhurya*).
An example:
*tāṃ tamālatarukāntilaṅghinīṃ kiṃkarīkṛtanavāmbudatviṣam* [She who surpasses the beauty of the *tamāla* tree and has reduced the luster of the fresh clouds to servitude.]
"Perceive within your own heart that Fortune who has long been kissed by the eyes of Naicikī, for the sake of your peace.
Or as it is said:
"Her cheeks are adorned with thick drops of perspiration, and she is worthy of salutation for her internal smiles and languid glances."
“A certain delightful state of the woman with intoxicating eyes, which sprouts joy through mere remembrance, arises in my mind.

In the first verse, because the longing for meditation on the Blessed One—or the love directed toward the Blessed One—which is adorned by the figure of speech *atiśayokti*, ultimately culminates in the *śānta* (quiescent) rasa, it manifests the *mādhurya* (sweetness) inherent in that [rasa]; in the second, however, it manifests the *mādhurya* belonging to the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) rasa supported by memory.

The *ojas* (vigorous) style of composition consists of a long-drawn structure that is closely knit together by sounds abundant in the second and fourth classes of consonants, the *ṭa*-class, the *ta*-class, the *jihvāmūlīya*, the *upadhmānīya*, the *visarga*, and the letter *sa*; and it is embraced by short vowels followed by conjuncts (*saṃyoga*) containing either a *jha*y- or a *ra*-sound, all employed in close proximity.

Those letters belonging to the first and third classes that fall under this [category] are neither favorable nor unfavorable to this quality, provided they do not constitute a *saṃyoga*; however, those that do constitute it are indeed favorable. The same applies to *anusvāra* and *parasavarṇa*.
As in the previously cited example beginning with "May this [arrow] fall mercilessly upon the shattered and arrogant..."—
the *ghaṭanā* (composition), which reveals the meaning of the sentence as clearly as a jujube fruit in the palm of one's hand upon merely being heard, is *prasāda* (clarity).
