however, they are not required in every respect as both the objective and the excitatory determinants (*ālambana-uddīpana*), as is the case with aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
However, if they are possible in some cases, they are not prohibited.

These include: joy (*harṣa*), memory (*smṛti*), shame (*vrīḍā*), delusion (*moha*), fortitude (*dhṛti*), apprehension (*śaṅkā*), exhaustion (*glāni*), dejection (*dainya*), anxiety (*cintā*), intoxication (*mada*), fatigue (*śrama*), pride (*garva*), sleep (*nidrā*), arrogance (*mati*), illness (*vyādhi*), fear (*trāsa*), dreaming (*supta*), awakening (*vibodha*), resentment (*amarṣa*), dissimulation (*avahittha*), ferocity (*ugratā*), madness (*unmāda*), death (*maraṇa*), deliberation (*vitarka*), despondency (*viṣāda*), longing (*autsukya*), agitation (*āvega*), stupor (*jaḍatā*), indolence (*ālasya*), envy (*asūyā*), epilepsy (*apasmāra*), and fickleness (*capalatā*).
There are thirty-three transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*), including "disgust" (*nirveda*) arising from self-reproach due to the influence of an antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
There are thirty-four [transitory states] when "attachment" (*rati*) directed toward objects such as teachers, deities, kings, and sons is included.
By this, the claim that there is a separate rasa called "affection" (*vātsalya*) based on objects such as one's children is refuted.
Because unrestrained behavior is refuted by the words of the sages,
in this context *harṣa* (joy) is a particular kind of pleasure arising from the attainment of what is desired and so forth.
Thus it has been said:
"The favor of gods, husband, teacher, or master; union with beloved ones;
the fulfillment of desires; and the acquisition of charming wealth that was previously unattainable."
Likewise, there is the arising of sons and so forth, as well as their disappearance;
furthermore, there is the clarity of the eyes and face, pleasant speech, and the bristling of the hair.
“Tears, perspiration, and so forth are the consequent emotions (anubhāvas); one should designate that [state] as joy.
An example:
“At the time of the day’s end, having reached the appointed hour, she fixed her eyes upon the door of the palace...”
"Then, upon seeing that I had arrived, the beautiful woman’s face blossomed.
Here, the arrival of the beloved at that specific time is the *vibhāva* (the excitant cause),
and the blossoming of her face is the *anubhāva* (the ensuant).
Memory is cognition produced by a mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
For example:
"That gentle, charming smile, those sighs, and that truly sweet splendor of her face, free from blemish—
even now they madden my heart, alas, for her whose eyes are like the lotus of evening."
In this case, the specific mental state (*cintā*) is the determinant cause (*vibhāva*).
The lowering of the eyebrows, the immobility of the limbs, and so forth, are the consequent effects (*anubhāvas*) to be understood through implication.
Although here [one might argue] it is simply this transitory emotion (*saṃcāribhāva*) of recollection (*smṛti*),...

Although it could be said that this constitutes *rasadhvani* due to the manifestation of the *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) rasa arising from the conjunction of the excitant (*vibhāva*) in the form of the heroine’s appearance and the ensuant (*anubhāva*) in the form of mental distress— conveyed by the word "alas" (*hanta*)— nevertheless, because it is recollection itself that is most immediately apparent and striking here, it is that which constitutes the *dhvani*.
It has been stated:

according to the view that the denotative power (śakti) of words such as "that" (tad) resides in that which is delimited by a mode present in the intellect, the intellect—serving merely as a unifier for the delimiters of denotability (śakyatāvacchedaka)—does not itself come into contact with the status of being the denoted (vācyatā).
Even according to the view that "being present in the intellect" is the delimiter of denotability, the intellect, by virtue of being a memory, is experienced solely as an individual (vyakti).

And although she is here to be understood through the sentence, because it is the word alone that possesses the nature of "producing" (kurvadrūpa), the object of the verbal expression is the word itself.
By this, the view that there is no aesthetic variety (*vaicitrya*) when entities are suggested by words is refuted.
Through the comparison with the evening lotus, the manifestation of her absorption in bliss is achieved by way of suggesting that her eyes are increasingly inclined toward closing.
“I remember for a long time the union with the woman, her neck bent low, her lotus-like tender eyes slightly closed, and her limbs languid from the weight of deep sighs.
In this instance, *smṛti* (remembrance) is not a *bhāva* (transitory emotion).
It is not [an instance of] suggestion (*vyaṅgya*), because it is expressed by its own word (*svaśabda*);
nor is it the figure of speech "recollection" (*smaraṇālaṃkāra*),
because it is not rooted in similarity (*sādṛśya*).

This is because of the established doctrine that only a recollection based on similarity constitutes a poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*), whereas any other [recollection] that is suggested (*vyañjita*) constitutes an emotion (*bhāva*).
However, since the excitant (*vibhāva*) itself is beautiful, it somehow culminates in rasa.

*Vrīḍā* (shame) is a particular state of mental modification arising from women’s gazing at the faces of men and so forth, or from men’s breaking their promises and suffering defeat and so forth; it is the cause of such effects as change of complexion and downcast eyes.
For example:
"Gazing very slowly at the nail-mark upon my chest between her two jar-like breasts, her body covered in horripilation..."
Seeing me with my face cast down, the young woman, her limbs trembling with alarm at the window, immediately entered her home.

In this context, the *vibhāva* consists of the sight of the beloved, as well as the sight of her horripilation and so forth, which communicate the joy produced by her perceiving the nail-marks of the beloved upon her breasts;
[and] her immediate entry into the house.
Anubhāva (the indicative):
Or for example—
“While he was offering a pigeon that was crying out before him, having swiftly intercepted the female pigeon as she was flying away...”
She slowly, very slowly, bent her lotus-face, moist with a smile, toward me.
Even here, as in the previous instance, joy—though present only in a slight degree—is indeed consistent with her bashfulness.
The *vibhāva* (the excitant cause) is the presentation of the female pigeon before the male by her beloved.
The bending of the face is the *anubhāva*.
Delusion (*moha*) is a state of mind that, being prompted by fear, separation, and so forth, fails to ascertain the true nature of reality;
however, the moderns maintain that it is "a state variegated by other conditions."
The example:
"With a heart distressed by separation, the young woman, lamenting 'O beloved, O beloved,' gazes at him even as he has arrived nearby, as if she were unfamiliar with him."
In this case, separation from the beloved is the *vibhāva* (the determinant cause);
the impairment of the senses and the absence of shame and so forth are the *anubhāvas* (the consequent effects).
Or, for example:
“Coiling his trunk like a ring on the bank of the river, with eyes slightly contracted,
the lordly elephant— bereft of his mate and devoid of purpose— neither draws up water nor plucks the cluster of lotuses.
Fortitude (*dhṛti*) is a specific state of mental modification that serves as the cause for warding off calamities produced by greed, grief, fear, and the like.
The example:
"Why do I torment my heart by running and running upon the surface of the earth? Do I have [any other recourse]?"
“The supreme Lord Nandakumāra is ever upon his head.
Here, discernment, the perfection of sacred learning, and so forth are the *vibhāvas* (determinants);
the subsiding of fickleness and other such traits is the *anubhāva* (consequent).

If it is asked: "But since there is no anxiety (*cintā*) in the second half [of the verse] because the object is clearly manifested, how can this be an expression of the state of composure (*dhṛti*)," [the answer is: because that [object] is manifested precisely for the sake of serving composure.
Anxiety (*śaṅkā*) is a particular modification of the mind characterized by the thought, "What undesirable thing will happen to me?"
The example:
“O friend, deceived by fate, I did not go to the appointed place of my beloved.
Alas, I know not now what King Kāma intends to do with me.”
In this case, the transgression against the king is the *vibhāva* (the determinant cause).
The change of facial color and so forth are the implied *anubhāvas* (consequent effects).
However, this [state] produces trembling and other such reactions by generating fear and the like, rather than being mere anxiety (*cintā*).

*Glāni* (depression) is a specific state of suffering arising from the loss of strength caused by mental or physical ailments; it is the cause of discoloration, looseness of the limbs, dizziness of the eyes, and so forth.
As it is said:
"Lying upon a bed of moss, she who remains only as a trace of beauty is like the crescent of the new moon."
"Even when her beloved has arrived nearby, she honors him only with sweet glances.
Here, the separation from the beloved is the *vibhāva* (the determinant).

The exclusion of actions such as rising to meet him, falling at his feet, or embracing him—implied by the particle *eva* ("only") in the phrase "only with sweet glances"—is the *anubhāva* (the consequent effect).
Nor should exhaustion be suspected here,
because of the absence of a cause;
however, some define *glāni* as the loss of strength arising from disease and so forth.
In their view, it should be considered how a wasting characterized by destruction can possibly occur within entities whose very nature consists of mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*).

Although the definition stating, "Wasting is the decline of strength arising from mental afflictions and physical diseases" indicates that destruction itself is understood by the term "decline," nevertheless,
due to the aforementioned logical inconsistency, it is precisely the suffering produced by the destruction of strength that is denoted by the term "decline of strength."

The intended meaning is as follows: *dainya* (dejection) is a specific modification of the mind that arises from suffering, poverty, offenses, and the like, and which serves as the cause for speaking of one's own inferiority and so forth.
An example:
"By me, a wretch, that lotus-eyed woman was suddenly banished into the depths of the forest;
where now is that virtuous lady to me, fallen as she is, like a supreme Sarasvatī?"
This is the speech of the venerable Śrī Rāmabhadra after he had abandoned Sītā.

Here, the abandonment of Sītā—either the offense itself or the sorrow arising from it—is the *vibhāva* (the determinant cause). His speech expressing self-depreciation through the comparison to a fallen person is the *anubhāva* (the consequent effect).
As they say:
"From anxiety, longing, mental distress, and the external stimulus of misfortune; and from the following internal effects: the turning back of the head and heaviness of the limbs."
"Through the abandonment of one's body and its ornaments, one should manifest the state of wretchedness (*dainya*).
And: "Wretchedness is a lack of luster caused by poverty and the like; it produces a state of filthiness and so forth.
Here, the fact that she was exiled by me, a wretch, and not by fate, is fully developed precisely through the simile of a fallen man.

But it is not by way of comparison with a Śūdra and so forth; for while the Śūdra’s lack of access to the Vedas is established by his very birth through the [cosmic] ordinance (*vidhi*), in the case of a fallen Brāhmaṇa or similar person, although the Vedas are easily accessible by nature according to the ordinance, he has himself distanced himself from the Vedas by committing such a sin. Thus, he is compared to the fallen one.
And here, the poetic figure of simile (*upamā*) based on the word *śrutya* (heard) embellishes her very wretchedness.

Likewise, through the two types of suggestion (*dhvani*) rooted in the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of the words *mayā* (by me) and *sā* (she), that same wretchedness is further nourished by the manifestation of numerous qualities such as ingratitude and gratitude, or mercilessness and compassion;
this occurs by means of the slight hint of remembrance conveyed by the word *sā*.

Cintā is a particular modification of the mind (cittavṛttiviśeṣa) produced by the attainment of the desired or the non-attainment of the undesired, and so forth; it is synonymous with anxiety (dhyāna) and is the cause of such states as discoloration, scratching the ground, and looking downward.
As they say:
"Wherein the determinants (vibhāvas) are poverty, the loss of power,
the constant deprivation of desired objects, frequent sighing and gasping, and a downward gaze."
Torment, remembrance, emaciation, lack of bodily grooming, and lack of fortitude are the external manifestations; that is proclaimed to be *cintā* (anxiety).
“Vitarka arises for this [mind] either in the preceding or the succeeding moment.
And: “Dhyāna is considered to be thought (cintā) that, because it does not attain what is beneficial, causes distress and so forth.
An example:

“The luster of her lower lip surpasses the new sprout; the beauty of her face exceeds the splendor of the moon; her body, for which no likeness has been made, was fashioned by the Creator—for whose sake?—of this fawn-eyed woman.
Here, the non-attainment of that [object] is the *vibhāva*.
The emotional states (anubhāvas) such as remorse and so forth are merely suggested;
nor should it be said that there is a suggestion of longing (autsukya) here.

For while a reflection whose object (ālambana) is an undetermined subject (dharmin)—expressed by the words "for whose sake?"—is indeed perceived, even though longing exists, it is not conveyed as the primary element by this sentence.

Intoxication (*mada*) is a specific modification of the mind characterized by exhilaration (*ullāsa*), born from the consumption of wine and other substances, and which is the cause of lying down, laughing, and so forth.
As they say:
"Intoxication, born from the consumption of liquor, is a mass of delusion and bliss."
In that regard, the manifestation of power in the highest person is sleep; in the middling, laughter and song;
but in the lowest, weeping, harsh speech, and so forth.
This intoxication is threefold, distinguished as young, middling, and low.
That which is enacted through indistinct and incoherent speech, and with a delicate, faltering gait, is the first.
The middling [intoxication] is characterized by the throwing of the arms, stumbling, reeling, and so forth;
the lowest is characterized by a breaking of gait, loss of memory, hiccups, and vomiting.
An illustration:
"Smiling most sweetly, speaking softly to himself about something,
this drunkard gazes at the three worlds as if they were devoid of any objective support.
Here, the consumption of intoxicating substances is the *vibhāva* (the determinant cause).
The inarticulate speech and so forth constitute the *anubhāva* (consequent emotion).

Here, because the description of the intoxicated nature has the purpose of manifesting the intoxication (*mada*) residing therein, the state of intoxication itself is the primary element; thus, the figure of speech *svabhāvokti* (description of nature) does not hold primacy, but rather serves merely as an embellishment for that *dhvani* (suggestive resonance).
Or again, here is another example:
“O young woman, place your sweet lower lip upon my face, for it is indeed as sweet as honey.
Take hold of my lotus-hand with your hand; alas, I shall fall, *papapa*, onto the ground, *bhabhab*!”
Here too, the same excitant (vibhāva) is present;
the emission of excessive syllables and so forth is the ensuant (anubhāva).

Furthermore, the vulgar expression found in the first half-verse, and in the second half-verse the description of one's own hand as being comparable to a lotus when it ought to be compared to the hand of a young woman, both serve only to nourish her intoxication.
Fatigue is a specific kind of exhaustion arising from extensive physical exertion, which serves as the cause for sighing, rubbing the limbs, sleep, and so forth.
As they say:
"By the determinants such as travel, physical exertion, and service; by the consequents such as massaging the limbs, contraction of the face, and twisting of the body;"
“Fatigue is considered to be characterized by sighs, slow yawning, and the lifting of the feet.
And: “Fatigue is exhaustion resulting from traveling on a journey and the like; it is considered to produce sleep, labored breathing, and so forth.
Furthermore, this arises even when strength is present.
And it arises from physical activity alone, not from exhaustion;
therefore, there is a distinction between exhaustion and fatigue.
The example:
“Having pressed her cheek against my face, that slender woman lay upon my heart; for a long time she was as if painted in a picture, unable even to stir slightly.”
In this case, the excitant (*vibhāva*) is the physical activity in the form of inverted sexual union;
the ensuants (*anubhāvas*) are the absence of movement, lying down, and so forth.
Nor should it be suspected that the purpose is already served by the suggestion (*dhvanana*) of the absence of sleep here.

For in deep sleep, due to the very absence of cognition, there is an absence of effort such that one is not even capable of the slightest movement; thus, [the presence of fatigue] would result in being devoid of purpose, and furthermore, since it is denoted by the verbal root *śīṅ* (to lie down/sleep), its status as a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) would be untenable.
However, in the case of physical exhaustion (*śrama*), its suitability is appropriate.
Pride (*garva*) is the contempt for others based on a cognition of self-exaltation that is occasioned by such things as physical beauty, wealth, or learning.
The example:
"From the base of the jewel-mountain [Meru] encircled by the Malaya range, down to the shore of the ocean—
let as many as there are who are skilled in composing poetry speak without hesitation."
"Who else but I is fortunate enough to experience the status of being a master of speech, which possesses the fortune of the sweetness of a smooth stream of flavor flowing from the heart of grapes?
Here, the awareness of the uniqueness of one's own poetry is the *vibhāva* (the determinative cause).
The utterance of such words directed at another’s disparagement is the *anubhāva* (consequent emotion);
moreover, even *asūyā* (envy) nourishes this slightly.
For the suggestion (*dhvani*) of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) is characterized primarily by energy (*utsāha*), yet possesses concealed pride (*gūḍhagarva*).
But this [heroic sentiment] is characterized primarily by pride; therefore, it is distinct from that [sentiment of wonder].

For instance, in the verse beginning with "yadi vakti" cited earlier in the context of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*), pride stands as the nourisher of the energy (*utsāha*) manifested by the statement, "I shall speak even together with Gīṣpati, the presiding deity of speech," and thus it prevails over all others.
Pride is the conceit that "I am superior to the wise";
it is not, however, as in the present verse, primarily perceived through a sarcastic statement such as "There is no one on earth other than me," which is explicitly uttered.
Sleep is the closing of the mind caused by fatigue and the like.
The closing of the eyes, the lack of activity in the limbs, and so forth are its consequent effects (*anubhāvas*).
An example:
"She, her joy increased by my arrival, spent the entire night in wakefulness."
"Though awakened by bees greedy for the fragrance of her breath in the morning, she did not wake.
Here, the fatigue from keeping a vigil at night is the *vibhāva* (the cause);
the lack of awakening despite the bees is the *anubhāva* (the effect).
*Matī* is the determination of an object produced by the investigation of the scriptures and so forth.
In this context, the following are the consequent manifestations (*anubhāvas*): freedom from doubt, the performance of actions for that purpose, the eradication of uncertainty, and so forth.
An example:
"The entire world is indeed perishable; moreover, within it, the body is utterly transient."
"Alas! For his sake, how much effort is being exerted by me!
Here, the contemplation of scriptures such as "This body is like a bubble on the water" constitutes the *vibhāva* (the determinants).
Self-reproach conveyed by the word "alas," the renunciation of royal service and the like, and freedom from craving constitute the *anubhāva* (the consequents).
The designation of "suggestion" (dhvani) applies to the *camatkāra* (aesthetic wonder) of the mother alone because it occurs instantaneously, and not to the son,
because his realization occurs with delay.
Illness is mental anguish arising from such things as separation from health.
Laxity of the limbs, labored breathing, and so forth are the consequent emotions (*anubhāvas*) here;
as it has been said:
"From the provocation of one, two, or all three [humors] individually or in pairs..."
The diseases arising from wind, bile, and phlegm are those such as fever and others.
In this context, that state arising from it is designated as "disease" (*vyādhi*).
An example:
"With moss clinging to her heart, she repeatedly tosses her limbs here and there."
She casts her gaze upon the faces of her friends, which are intent on news of him, yet exceedingly dejected.
Here, separation (*viraha*) is the *vibhāva* (the determinant cause),
and the tossing of limbs and so forth is the *anubhāva* (the consequent effect).
Fear (*trāsa*) is a particular modification of the mental state (*cittavṛttiviśeṣa*) arising in a timid person from seeing a terrifying creature, hearing a thunderclap, or similar causes.
And its manifestations (anubhāvas) are horripilation, trembling, paralysis, dizziness, and so forth;
as it is said:
"Fear caused by portents is a distraction of the mind that brings about trembling and other such effects."
The example:
“In the company of her friends, the young girl, through her impetuosity for play, repeatedly reproached my speech;
yet, having heard from afar my voice, which was as beautiful as lightning, she became possessed of exquisite splendor.”
In this instance, the husband’s hearing of his own words is the *vibhāva* (the excitant),
and her flight is the *anubhāva* (the ensuant).
Furthermore, one should not suspect that shame (*lajjā*) is what is suggested (*vyaṅgya*) here.
Because she was rejected by him while still a child;
or rather, this is a distinct example:
"O compassionate one, do not whip me with your lotus-hand; my heart trembles."
"O Mother, I shall never cause delay for the cowherd boys while playing.
This is the speech of the Blessed One, the youthful cowherd in his divine play.
Sleep is the knowledge arising from the determinants (vibhāva) of drowsiness.
"Sleep" refers to dreaming; its manifestations are such things as incoherent speech (pralāpa) and the like.
However, the closing of the eyes and so forth are manifestations of sleep itself, not of this [dreaming].
Because it is not produced by anything else (*anidaṃjanya*).

As for what was stated by the predecessors—"The experience of this [state] consists of the steady posture of the limbs and the closing of the eyes," and so forth—it should be understood that although those [physical signs] may be established through other means, they nonetheless pervade this particular state (*bhāva*).
An example—
“O pitiless one, O ocean of false speech, release the hem of my garment!”— thus speaking,
the slender woman, her ornaments cast aside and tears flowing incessantly, declared, “I have truly experienced your affection.”
"O auspicious Nidrā, who here could have informed [him] of you, were it not for you?
This is the speech of someone who, having seen his beloved speaking in such a manner even in a dream while he was away on a journey, addresses Nidrā.
Although the underlying fact (*vastu*) is that "by reporting my beloved's condition in such a state, O Nidrā, you have rendered me a great service," [the verse continues:]
Although the sentiment of love-in-separation (vipralambha-śṛṅgāra) also enters the path of perception here,
nevertheless, because it presents itself most prominently at the outset, the suggestion of a dream is cited as the primary instance;
this does not prevent the suggestion of those two [sentiments] from occurring at the conclusion.
Vibodha is the awakening that arises subsequent to the loss of sleep.
The loss of sleep and its restoration arise from powerful sounds, touches, and so forth occurring at the end of a dream; therefore, these alone are the excitants (*vibhāva*) here.
Rubbing the eyes, massaging the limbs, and so forth are the consequents (*anubhāva*).
In that regard:
A brief example:
"Alas! While I was being informed by sleep—so beneficial to me—during the final watch of the night, just as I was hearing the words of my fair-eyed beloved, a rain-cloud burst forth."
In this context, the hearing of thunder is the *vibhāva* (the determinant cause).
The resulting joy upon hearing the beloved’s words is the *anubhāva* (the consequent effect), which is to be inferred.
Some authorities maintain that this [joy] is also produced by the destruction of ignorance (*avidyā*). According to their view—
“The delusion is destroyed, memory has been regained by me through Your grace, O Acyuta;
I stand firm with all doubt dispelled, and I shall do as You command.
Thus should this verse from the Gītā be cited.

However, it should not be suspected that the meaning of the sentence here consists solely of indignation directed at the cloud; for only when awakening is perceived— and when the impropriety therein is understood— is indignation toward the cloud perceived as a delayed consequence, namely, because it produces such an improper awakening,
since [indignation] depends upon looking to another's face.
There might also be primacy for that [dream] if there were anything at all within the dream that indicated mercilessness and so forth on the part of the rain-cloud;
nor is there such primacy for the dream itself.
For by the cry of the water-carrier, only its destruction is understood.
Or, let there be a commingling of this [sentiment] with the state of dreaming and with envy;
however, this [following example] should not be cited:
“Having embraced her tightly, who had stayed with him throughout the entire night,
he abandoned sleep in the morning and then embraced consciousness.
This is because awakening is denoted by the term *cetanā*.

Just as someone who has made a truthful promise, having given two heroines to two different times for enjoyment, enjoys one at the appropriate time and, when the other time arrives, leaves her and enjoys the other—
in the same way, this [state] is manifested here by the very concise expression (*samāsokti*) that "at night there is sleep, and in the morning there is consciousness.

Envy (*amarṣa*) is a particular modification of the mental state (*cittavṛtti*) caused by various offenses such as the contempt shown by another, which serves as the cause for silence, verbal harshness, and so forth.
As before,
the causes and effects are respectively the determinants (vibhāva) and the consequents (anubhāva).
An example—

"Having touched the tips of the breasts with her hand, as her beloved suddenly moved far away, the passionate woman remained silent, silent, and indeed silent, gazing with her eyes whose corners were red at the lotus-face of her lover. Here, however, the sudden touch of the tips of the breasts is the *vibhāva* (the excitant).
Redness of the eyes and a fixed, unblinking gaze are the consequent emotions (*anubhāva*).

If it is asked, "What is the distinguishing factor between the two stable (*sthāyin*) and transitory (*saṃcārin*) emotions, namely anger (*krodha*) and resentment (*amarṣa*)?", understand that the difference lies solely in their distinct objective referents (*viṣayatā*).

In that context, however, the indicators are the immediate engagement in the destruction of others and so forth, as well as the turning away from speech and the like; thus, there is a distinction in the resulting effect (*kārya*).
*Avahittha* is a particular state of mind produced for the purpose of concealing the manifesting emotions (*anubhāva*) such as joy through causes such as shame.
As it has been said:
"The emotion called *avahittha* is said to be for the purpose of concealing an experience;
it is manifested through fear, shame, impudence, crookedness, and gravity."
For example:
"Having heard from the elders during a conversation with the cowherds about the greatness of the Lord of the Yadus, a virtuous wife, her cheeks perspiring and bristling with thrill..."
Upon the hood of the lord of serpents, who suddenly vomits forth a mass of blazing poison-flames,
he describes with great wonder the manner of his dance; here,
shame is the excitant (*vibhāva*).
An anecdote concerning such a person like Kāliya is an *anubhāva* (consequent emotion).
In this same way, examples prompted by fear and so forth may also be cited.
*Ugratā* (fierceness) is a mental state arising from insults, humiliation, and the like, taking the form of thoughts such as "What shall I do to him? and so on.
As they say:

"Offense against the king, the proclamation of false faults, and being held as a thief—these may be the *vibhāvas* (excitants); furthermore, imprisonment, execution, beating, breaking, and threats [are the consequents]."
“Where these [emotions] are the manifesting conditions (*anubhāva*), there is that ferocity consisting of mercilessness.
For example:
“Having indeed suffered defeat on the field of battle, this is truly a most inauspicious omen for the Lord of Aṅga...”
"Your heart does not tremble as you disparage my Gāṇḍīva bow, which has surpassed the power of others.
This is Dhananjaya’s speech directed toward Yudhiṣṭhira, who was disparaging the Gāṇḍīva after it had been defeated by Karṇa;
here, the disparagement of the Gāṇḍīva committed by Yudhiṣṭhira constitutes the *vibhāva* (the excitant cause).
It is the manifestation of the desire to kill.
Nor should it be said that there is no difference between indignation (*amarṣa*) and ferocity (*ugratā*),
because in the previously cited instance of the suggestion of indignation (*amarṣadhvani*), ferocity was not perceived.
Nor is this [state] anger (*krodha*),
because there is a distinction between that [anger] as a stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) and this [madness] as a transitory emotion (*saṃcāribhāva*).
Madness (*unmāda*) is the appearance of one thing as another, arising from such states as separation, great calamity, or supreme bliss.
The phrase ending with "birth" (*janma*) is used to exclude cognitions such as that of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
An example [of this type of cognition] is:
“O heartless beloved, I release you from here; henceforth I shall not [be yours].”

Thus she speaks, distressed, taking the lotus-hand of her female companion. This is the speech of a certain messenger to a hero who is asking about the condition of his own mistress while he is away on a journey; here, the separation from the beloved is the *vibhāva* (the determinant cause).
Incoherent speech is an *anubhāva*.
Although madness (*unmāda*) can be included within the category of disease (*vyādhi*), its separate mention is intended to highlight its specific distinctness from other diseases.
Death is the state preceding actual death, consisting of fainting and caused by illness and other such factors.
And in this context, it is not appropriate to understand "death" in its primary sense as the separation from life-breath (*prāṇa*),
because such a thing is impossible in the case of mental states, which consist of fluctuations of consciousness (*cittavṛtti*).
Furthermore, in all entities, the conjunction of the body and the life-breath functions as the cause by way of co-existence with the effect.
The example:
"She who was just now seen upon her bed recollecting the virtues of her beloved— alas,
that slender-limbed woman does not respond even when addressed."
In this case, the separation from a beloved is the *vibhāva* (the determinant cause),

and the cessation of speech is the *anubhāva* (the ensuant effect). Because the word "alas" (*hanta*) is so extremely contributory here, this emotion, although suggested by the sentence as a whole, attains the status of being suggested by the word.
By this, the claim that there is no ultimate poetic uniqueness (*vaicitrya*) when a state of being (*bhāva*) is suggested by words is refuted.
The fact (*vastu*) suggested by the phrase "recollecting the virtues of her beloved"— namely, that "even in her final state, she did not forget the virtues of her beloved"—
serves to nourish either the *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) or the sorrow (*śoka*) manifested at the very end.

And this state [of the hero] is nourished by a subsequent sentence within the composition that serves as its own manifestor; the distinction is that it nourishes *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) when describing the restoration of the heroine and so forth, but otherwise it nourishes *karuṇa* (pathos). Poets, moreover, do not describe this [sentiment] as the primary focus.
Because it consists primarily of inauspiciousness,
*vitarka* (speculative reasoning) is that which arises immediately after doubt and other such states.
And that [thought] was conducive to certainty:
"If that daughter of the Lord of Mithilā does not exist at all upon this earth, then how can there be life for me? For there is no standing for one who relies on anything without a support."
This is the speech of the Blessed Lord Rāma regarding himself.
The doubt as to whether Sītā exists on earth or not is the *vibhāva* (the determinant cause) here.
The dancing of the eyebrows, head, and fingers is the implied *anubhāva* (the consequent effect).
Nor can it be said that this [future object] is an object of thought,
because thought— taking such forms as "What will happen? or "How will it happen?"— is not invariably a cause for certainty.
And because one perceives a distinction from the object in the form of a deliberation (*vitarka*) such as "this ought to be thus,
for the most part," the *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a different fact) expressed in the verse beginning with "not without" (*na vinā*) is also appropriate in this context.
Despair (*viṣāda*) is remorse produced by the transgression of a beloved, a king, a teacher, or others.
The example:
"Now that the son of Bhāskara has set and the excellence of the Pāṇḍavas has arisen,
O life of Duryodhana, why do you not depart even now?"
In this context, the perception of one's own degradation and the excellence of another is the *vibhāva* (the determinant cause).
The hope for the departure of life,
along with the resulting lowering of the face and so forth, is the *anubhāva* (the consequent effect).

And within this very path of the suggestion of despondency (*viṣādadhvani*), the suggestion whose expressed meaning is transferred to another sense (*arthāntarasaṃkramitavācyadhvani*)— namely, "of Duryodhana"— acts as a supporting element.
Nor can it be claimed here that there is a suggestion of the emotion of fear (*trāsabhāvadhvani*), because even a trace of fear is incompatible with Duryodhana, who is a hero among enemies.
Nor does it have the tone of anxiety, because his resolve is "I shall die after fighting";
nor does it have the tone of dejection.
Even though there is the destruction of the entire army, because he does not take those calamities into account,

this is either not an instance of the suggestion of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa-dhvani*), since there is an absence of the energy (*utsāha*) that seeks life through the humiliation of the enemy by resorting to death.
Furthermore, this should not be cited here:
"O, slacken the speed of these merciless horses swift as the wind; I do not wish to witness the battle."
These cries of the kṣatriyas, whose arms resemble the coils of enraged serpents, tear apart the openings of my ears.
In this case, since only fear (*trāsa*) is perceived and despondency (*viṣāda*) is not perceived;
or, even if it were perceived as a mere trace (*leśa*), because fear alone would be appropriate, the work would be unfit for the designation of *dhvani*.
The desire that "may I obtain this very thing right now" is longing (autsukya).
In this context, the separation from a beloved and so forth are the determinants (vibhāva); haste, anxiety, and so forth are the consequents (anubhāva).
As they say:
“Born from separation from the beloved, it was inflamed by the recollection of the lover, and further intensified by sleep, lethargy, heaviness of limb, and anxiety.”
“Eagerness has been defined and described by those skilled in the nature of aesthetic emotion (bhāva).
For example:
“With tears falling and checked, and with pupils possessing a tremulousness as it was spoken...”
"When shall I behold the blue-lotus eyes of the deer-eyed one?
This is *āvega* (agitation), a mental state characterized by a flurry born from an excess of misfortune.
The example:
“He who effortlessly bound the ocean—that very joy of the Raghu dynasty approaches!
Where shall I go, O Daśānana, you whose wicked sports are born of pride? Destruction of the lineage is at my side!”
This is the speech of Mandodarī regarding herself.
Here, the arrival of the descendant of Raghu is the *vibhāva* (the excitant).
"Where shall I go?"—this suggests the *anubhāva* (the ensuant) of instability.
Nor can it be said that anxiety is primarily manifested here,
because anxiety is not perceived since agitation— clearly recognized through the lack of stability— is what is actually conveyed, such as by the thought, "Where shall I go?
However, in the savoring of the agitation, anxiety also becomes an object of experience as a subordinate quality (guṇa) by virtue of its role in nourishing that [agitation].

Lethargy (*jaḍatā*) is a state of mental fluctuation devoid of the application of mind toward necessary duties, arising from anxiety, longing, fear, separation, or the sight and hearing of the liked and disliked.
And this [ignorance] arises from delusion both before and after;
as it is said:
"Incapacity for discerning cause and effect is dullness, even for one who sees or hears."
Its determinants (vibhāvas) are the sight or hearing of the beloved or the disagreeable, and physical pain.

The *anubhāvas*, however, are silence, loss of composure, forgetfulness, and so forth. It is the opinion of the learned that such [confusion] may occur either before or after [the realization], due to delusion (*moha*). An example: * *tūṣṇīṃbhāva-vismaraṇādayaḥ* (silence, forgetfulness, and so forth) * *sā* (that [confusion]) * *pūrvaṃ* (before) * *parataḥ* (after) * *vā* (or) * *syāt* (may occur) * *mohāt* (due to delusion) * *iti* (thus) * *vidāṃ matam* (the opinion of the learned) * *udāharaṇam* (example)
“O companion, from the moment my beloved came to be far away by the power of fate, from that moment on, my senses have slackened their devotion to their own functions.
Here, separation from the beloved is the *vibhāva* (the determinant cause).
The *anubhāva* (consequent effect) is the loosening of the inclination toward specific cognitions regarding their respective objects through the instruments of perception, such as the eyes and ears.
In the case of delusion (*moha*), there is a non-occurrence of visual and other perceptions by means of the eyes and so forth;
however, the distinction here is that it is characterized by a specific mode and occurs predominantly as a non-occurrence. Therefore, this [state] is distinct from that.

For this very reason, it is said that [the mind] is "slackened" in the example, and not "abandoned. Laziness (ālasya) is the mind's lack of inclination toward action, produced by extreme satiety, internal disease, fatigue, and so forth.
And here, there is neither incapacity nor a lack of discrimination between what ought and ought not to be done;

therefore, even though the underlying emotion (*anubhāva*) consisting in the non-performance of duty is the same, there is a distinction between this [state] and languor (*glāni*) or insensibility (*jaḍatā*).
An example:
"Awakened by stories told by her beloved who had arrived from afar after an entire night..."
“I am truly unable to say more, my friend; do not speak, for your tongue is made of iron.

This is the speech of a certain woman, overcome by the languor born of staying awake all night, addressed to her friend who repeatedly asks about the events of the night on the second day after her beloved’s arrival.
Herein, staying awake all night is the *vibhāva* (the excitant).
The absence of excessive conversation is the *anubhāva*.
Another distinction is that in the case of insensibility (*jaḍatā*), being preceded by or following upon delusion (*moha*) is necessary, but this is not so here.

Since this is a subject to be kept secret, if the phrase "by means of stories" (*kathābhiḥ*) is intended as having an unintended literal meaning (*avivakṣitavācya*), then let there be "fatigue" (*śrama*) as the nourishing factor (*paripoṣaka*).

For when laziness (*ālasya*) is produced by fatigue, the fact that fatigue acts as its nourisher is unavoidable. However, it should be understood that when laziness is produced by excessive satiety and the like, its object is distinct from that of fatigue.
Envy (*asūyā*) is a specific modification of the mind (*cittavṛttiviśeṣa*) arising from seeing the excellence of others and so forth, which serves as the cause for reviling others and the like.
They express this very thing through words such as "intolerance" (*asahanā*),
as for example:
"Where is this Śaiva bow, and where is this ordinary child?"
"But destruction was brought about solely by Time, the destroyer of all.
This is the speech of the local kings who could not endure the prowess of the Blessed Lord Rāma, who broke the bow of Śiva.
Here, the "vibhāva" (the excitant cause) is the manifestation of the supreme excellence of the glorious strength of the son of Daśaratha.
The expression of the sentiment (anubhāva) is accessible even to the words of ordinary children:

"While the flocks of cakora birds, their eyes restless with thirst, gaze toward the eastern quarter; while the clusters of night-lotuses abandon their silence; and while the God of Love twangs his bow—"
"O Creator, now that the pride of proud women is suddenly about to depart, why indeed is this display of clouds appropriate for the rite [of parting]?
Here too, although there is the manifestation of censure— consisting of improper conduct— brought about by the perception of her unrestrained behavior and so forth, [the intended meaning remains].
It can indeed be said that the poet's resentment directed toward the Creator is suggested;

nevertheless, because the cause and the effect are identical, this [resentment] is perceived as being colored by the manifested indignation itself, rather than being apprehended in its pure, distinct form.
For there is no fault in the Blessed Lord Rāma comparable to the fault of the Creator, by which indignation might be manifested even among heroes, as it is in the case of poets;
for the very nature of heroes is the accomplishment of highly exalted deeds.

It should not be argued that because the narrative of the relevant princes is suggested here through the narrative of the irrelevant moon, this does not constitute the suggestion of indignation (*asūyā-dhvani*).
Because one sound is not in contradiction with another sound;

otherwise, there would never be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the sound of a great sentence and the sounds of intermediate sentences, nor between those and the sounds of words.
Apasmāra is a specific type of disease arising from an excess of separation, grief, fear, disgust, and so forth, as well as from possession by malevolent spirits and the like.

Even though this has already been mentioned by way of being "sick," it is stated again in its specific form to clarify that, among the *bībhatsa* (the loathsome) and *bhayānaka* (the terrifying), only this particular disease serves as a constituent element (*aṅga*), and no other;
however, in the case of *vipralambha* (love-in-separation), other types of diseases may also serve as such elements.
An example follows:
"Having heard that Hari, the destroyer of Death himself, had arrived at Mathurā,
Kaṃsa, trembling and gasping, fell to the ground.
Here, fear is the *vibhāva* (the determinant cause).
Trembling, sighing, falling [of the body], and so forth are the consequent expressions (*anubhāva*).
*Capalatā* (restlessness) is a mental state that serves as the cause for verbal harshness and the like, which are produced by indignation and other such emotions.
As it has been said:
"Impatience, hostility, envy, passion, hatred, and avarice—these are the excitants (*vibhāva*); while verbal abuse is the ensuant (*anubhāva*)."
“Harshness of speech, striking, beating, killing, and binding— that is considered rashness,
which consists in acting without due reflection. Thus it is said.
The example:
“O you of evil vows, O wicked-souled one, do not show me your face in this way!
I wish to destroy myself by that very thing through which you have been brought forth.”
This is the speech of Hiraṇyakaśipu to Prahlāda, who sees no means of thwarting his devotion to the Blessed One.

Here, the "vibhāva" (the excitant) is the hatred for his son, which has been aroused by his hatred for the Blessed One. The "anubhāvas" (the ensuants) are his desire for his own son's death and his harsh words.
Nor should it be argued that only indignation (*amarṣa*) is manifested here;

for since Hiraṇyakaśipu’s indignation toward Prahlāda—who has always been devoted to the Lord—has been accumulated over a long period, it is illogical for the desire to kill him to be his first occurrence.

Furthermore, because a first-time effect must be produced by a first-time cause, there is established a distinct mental state called fickleness (*capalatā*), which differs from his previous mental dispositions.
Nor should it be said that it is only the intensity of indignation (*amarṣa*) that manifests as the cause for the desire to kill oneself and so forth;
for since even intensity must necessarily possess a specific, inherent characteristic, that very [intensity] is what constitutes the referent of the term *capalatā* (fickleness/immoderation),
especially in the case of base persons.

Nirveda is a state of mind characterized by aversion toward sense objects, produced by such things as verbal abuse, insults, illness, beatings, poverty, separation from loved ones, or witnessing the prosperity of others; furthermore, it may be produced by contempt and the like directed toward superiors. It manifests through weeping, long sighs, a dejected countenance, and so forth. An example follows:
“If, O Lakṣmaṇa, that deer-eyed woman does not enter the path of my vision,
what is the use of this dull life of mine or of this world that has become fruitless?
Because it lacks the quality of being produced from the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal objects, this [sentiment] is not the cause for the designation of *rasa*.
An example of passion directed toward objects such as the gods is as follows: “Before your gate,
[the serpent] whose hoods are split by the blows of the staffs of the wrathful Jaya and Vijaya...”
“Those crowns—Brahmā, Mahendra, and the rest—are like mere insects;
they stand there as wretched things, longing for the falling glance of your eyes.
What are those lords of heaven, whose lives have been extinguished, compared to that?”

In this case, it might be argued that the love (rati) directed toward the Blessed One—which resides in Brahmā and others—is not manifested through such means as enduring insults, attending upon the door of the Blessed One, or longing for the falling of the Blessed One’s sidelong glances; rather, it is because the Blessed One’s sovereignty transcends the reach of speech and mind. Even so, the status of this as *dhvani* remains entirely intact, as it is manifested by the poet’s own love directed toward the Blessed One, which is itself evoked by the description of such divine sovereignty.
Or take this example:

"I do not beg for wealth, nor for the prosperity of a kingdom, nor indeed for knowledge; O Lord, I ask for only this one thing: cast upon me even a slight glance, rippling with the waves of compassion."
In this context, the longing for the fall of the Lord’s glance upon one who is devoid of expectation for wealth and the like indeed manifests absolute devotion toward the Blessed One.
Thus have the *bhāvas* been described in brief.
Now, how is the restriction of their number established?

If it is argued that this is because [other states] such as stinginess (*mātsarya*), agitation (*udvega*), hypocrisy (*dambha*), envy (*īrṣyā*), lack of discernment (*aviveka*), certainty (*nirṇaya*), timidity (*klaibya*), forbearance (*kṣamā*), curiosity (*kutuka*), longing (*utkaṇṭhā*), modesty (*vinaya*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), and audacity (*dhārṣṭya*) are also observed in various instances of literary expression, we say:
no; for since these are included within those already mentioned, no other number is possible.
From envy comes parsimony;
from fear, agitation;
and from the state known as dissimulation, hypocrisy.
From indignation comes envy; from discernment comes determination;
and from dejection comes impotence.
Of steadfastness and forbearance,
of eagerness and curiosity,
of modesty and decorum.

Because doubt arises from reasoning and audacity from impulsiveness, although there is in fact a subtle distinction between them, one determines [the latter] as not distinct from the former due to its necessary connection;
for it is impossible to observe the words of the Sage while being unrestrained, as that would be improper.
And among these transitory mental states (*saṃcāribhāva*), some serve as the determinants (*vibhāva*) or the consequents (*anubhāva*) for others;
for instance, envy (*īrṣyā*) serves as the determinant for despondency (*nirveda*).
The state of being an *anubhāva* (consequent) with respect to envy (*asūyā*),

the state of being a *vibhāva* (determinant) with respect to sleep (*nidrā*) for [the emotion] of anxiety (*cintā*), and the state of being an *anubhāva* with respect to longing (*autsukya*), and so forth, should be inferred by oneself.

Now, regarding the semblance of rasa (rasābhāsa): therein, the state of being a semblance of rasa consists in having an inappropriately chosen objective basis (ālambana) for the determinants (vibhāva).
Furthermore, impropriety regarding the *vibhāva* (the excitants) and other factors is to be understood from the worldly conduct of people;
some say it is that wherein they have the notion "this is improper.
Others do not accept that.

Even if [the definition] were to include passion (*rati*) and so forth directed toward the wives of sages and the like, it would still fail to include passion directed toward multiple lovers or passion that resides in neither [of the two parties].
This is because, in those cases, there is no lack of propriety (*anaucitya*) residing in the excitants (*vibhāva*).
Therefore, passion and the other [emotions] must be qualified by a lack of propriety.
And thus, this includes [the cases] where the excitants (*vibhāva*) are inappropriate, where the object is multiple heroes, and where [the emotion] does not culminate in either [hero].
Inappropriateness (*anaucitya*) is exactly as described before;
in that context, the state of being a semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*) is not co-referential with the state of being actual rasa (*rasatva*), and so forth.
Because that which is stainless alone possesses the nature of *rasa* and so forth.
Some say: "It is like [the status of] being a fallacy of reason (*hetvābhāsa*) while [still] being a reason.
For there is no loss of self-identity merely through unfamiliarity.
"However, others maintain that because they possess defects, they are designated as 'appearances' (ābhāsa), just like the designation of 'horse-appearances' and so forth. An example follows:
By some means, through a hundred stratagems, he reached the top of the palace;
there, having awakened his slender-limbed beloved— who was lying in secret on a bed of flowers, pure as the foam of nectar, her eyes startled and her face smiling— [he embraced her].
"Ah! The fortunate man embraces the queen with a sigh.
Here, the *ālambana* (the objective basis) is the queen, who has shown improper affection;
the *uddīpana* (the excitants), such as the secret night, serves to intensify it.
The anubhāvas are the king’s rash entry into the inner apartments, his disregard for his own life, and his sighing, embracing, and so forth.
Doubt and the like are transitory emotions (saṃcāribhāvas). Furthermore, because this erotic sentiment (rati) has a prohibited object as its basis, the rasa is merely a semblance (ābhāsa).

Nor should it be argued that the phrase "with startled eyes" implies a fear of contact with another man, thereby suggesting that the erotic sentiment (*rati*) does not reside in both parties and thus constitutes a flaw (*ābhāsatā*).

For this woman has been attached to him for a long time; since the arrival of another man in the inner apartments is utterly impossible, her initial fear—expressed in the thought, "Who is this awakening me?"—is entirely appropriate.

Subsequently, as their intimacy is revealed, she smiles, manifesting the joy born from the realization: "This is my beloved, who has come for my sake, regarding even his own life as a mere blade of grass. Thus, the phrase "with a smiling face" [is justified].
The qualification also reveals her love;
however, primacy belongs solely to the love residing in the hero, because that constitutes the entire meaning of the sentence.
Or as it is said:
"Then the young girl, entering the palace with compassion, cast a garland of lotus-eyes upon the youths who were languidly longing for even a slight portion of the command to depart on the road."

In this context, when a certain woman was being followed on the road by young men whose minds were captivated by her beauty and youth as she approached from somewhere, at the moment of her entering the house, there arose among them— those who were eager for the gain of being commanded to depart so that they might realize the fruitfulness of their own service— a gesture consisting of the casting of a garland of lotus-eyes, which was an *anubhāva* (consequent emotion) born of compassion arising from the recollection of their extreme exhaustion, serving as a communication of the command to depart.

Since *rati* (erotic passion) is manifested through description, it is understood from the use of the plural number (*bahuvacanena*) as having many objects; thus, this too constitutes a semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*).
Or, for example:
“The newly wed bride was taken into the cage of her husband’s arms.”
She trembles excessively like a young doe fallen into a net at that moment.
Here, because the passion (*rati*) has not touched the new bride even slightly, it is an "appearance" (*ābhāsa*) due to its non-abiding in either [of the two].
As it has been said:

"In the case of a woman who has another man as her lover, or one who has gone to the wife of a sage or a guru, or in sexual intercourse involving many men, as well as in that which is established in neither [of these]," so it is said.
Here, by the words "sage" (muni) and "guru," others such as the king are also implied by way of illustration.
[This is] the apprehension.
Now, what is manifested here?— “Bent low, trembling, and indeed wide-open, [the eyes] are utterly agitated.”
"The first glances of the princess of Pañcāla fall upon the sons of Pāṇḍu.
Here, through his state of being bowed down, there is devotion toward Yudhiṣṭhira, prompted by his righteousness;
and through his state of being agitated, there is trepidation toward Bhīmasena, prompted by his massive form.

The modern scholars maintain that this is merely a semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*), because the princess of Pañcāla manifests through her glances— which reveal Arjuna’s joy induced by hearing of his extraordinary heroism due to their wide-open gaze, and the eagerness of Nakula and Sahadeva induced by his supreme beauty due to their state of extreme agitation— the love directed toward multiple objects.
However, some authorities maintain that when there are many suitors or many leaders, the *rati* (erotic passion) is merely a semblance (*ābhāsa*).

In that regard, just as the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) is twofold, so too is the semblance of the erotic (*śṛṅgārābhāsa*), distinguished by the categories of union (*saṃyoga*) and separation (*vipralambha*).
The semblance of union has just been illustrated immediately above.
An example of the semblance of deception is as follows:
"At one moment he speaks incoherently, and at another moment he resorts to silence."
Moreover, he directs his gaze without any support upon every object;
he takes long breaths and does not maintain even the slightest steadiness in his limbs— alas, the Lord of Laṅkā is swallowed up by the loveliness of Vaidehī!

In this instance, this *vipralambha-rati* (love-in-separation) directed toward the Lord of Laṅkā and having Sītā as its objective support has attained the status of a semblance (*ābhāsa*) because it does not culminate in both [the lover and the beloved] and because its object is the wife of the Preceptor of the World; likewise, the madness, exhaustion, delusion, anxiety, and disease manifested through expressions such as "she speaks perversely" have likewise attained the status of semblances. Being primarily nourished by these, it serves as the basis for the designation of *dhvani*. Similarly, grief (*śoka*) described as having a quarrelsome son or the like as its objective support, and as being grounded in those who are free from passion (*vītarāga*), [is also a semblance].

Disgust arises from the fact that the knowledge of Brahman is beyond the reach of outcastes and the like; anger and energy arise from their presence in the miserly, the cowardly, and so forth, or from taking one's father and others as objects; and wonder arises from taking magicians and the like as objects.
Furthermore, laughter based on the teacher and others,
fear arising from the state of being a great hero,
and disgust described through the objects of sacrificial animal fat, blood, flesh, and so forth, are semblances of rasa (rasābhāsa).
These have not been cited here for fear of prolixity; they should be inferred by the wise.
In this very way, there are mere semblances of emotion (*bhāvābhāsa*) whose objects are inappropriate, such as:
All objects of the senses have passed into the path of oblivion, and even my learning, overcome by exhaustion, has turned away;
there remains for me only that girl with eyes like those of a young fawn.
It never departs from the heart, like a presiding deity.

This is the utterance of someone— either another man whose mind was captivated by the beauty of the teacher’s daughter during his period of study at the *gurukula*, or perhaps the teacher himself— who has gone to another land while remembering her who was not forbidden to him;
here, through the abandonment or non-abandonment of his own self, he expresses ingratitude toward objects such as garlands and sandalwood, as well as toward the long-practiced knowledge.
And since the transcendence (*lokottaratva*) manifested in this [comparison] nourishes only the memory of its distinct nature (*vyatirekavapuḥ-smṛti*), that [memory] alone is primary.
Thus, even the comparison with the presiding deity (*adhidevatopamā*) serves to manifest the quality of being perpetual, which resides in the absence of abandonment.
Furthermore, because its object is inappropriate and because it does not reside in both [the subject and the object], this is a semblance of emotion (*bhāvābhāsa*).
If, however, this is the statement of the one who transforms it, then it is indeed a suggestion of existence (*bhāvadhvani*).
Now, the pacification of existence (bhāvaśānti): it is the pacification—that is, the destruction—of existence, whose nature was described previously.
And it (the suggested meaning) is to be grasped precisely as delimited by its arising, for only that [moment] produces aesthetic wonder in the connoisseur.
An example—
"O passionate lady, you still do not release your anger; yet the row of clouds has already risen.
By these words of her husband, the crimson glow from the corners of the slender woman's lotus-eyes was quenched.
Here, the hearing of such beloved words is the *vibhāva*.

The destruction of the red luster located in the corners of the eyes, or the serenity manifested by that [destruction], is the transitory emotion (anubhāva). The destruction of anger delimited by the time of its arising is the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya).
Likewise—*bhāvodayaḥ* is the arising of a state; that is, the production of a state.
The example:
"Beholding upon her husband's chest the mark of his rival's lover’s necklace,
the beautiful woman instantly drew back her vine-like arm, which had been looped around the region of his shoulder."
Here too, the perception of the mark of the rival lover’s necklace upon the breast of her beloved is the *vibhāva* (the excitant).
The drawing back of her own vine-like arm, which had been encircled as a bracelet around the region of her beloved’s side, is the *anubhāva* (the ensuant).
The arising of anger is the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).
Even though, because the emergence of another entity is necessary upon the cessation of one entity,

or the cessation of a prior entity is necessary upon the emergence of an entity, these two are not distinct objects of conventional discourse; nevertheless, because there is an absence of aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) when both occur in a single instance, [they are distinguished].
And because worldly transaction depends upon wonder,
there is a distinction of objects;
thus—
The conjunction of states (*bhāvasaṃdhi*) is the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of two states that are not mutually overwhelmed, yet are capable of mutual overwhelming.
The example:
"At Rāghava, the lotus-glories of Janakī’s eyes— excessively apprehensive of the onset of youth, yet enticed by his character, heroism, strength, and loveliness— contract and expand."

Here, the perception of the emergence of superhuman youthfulness residing in the Blessed Lord Rāma, as well as his corresponding virtue, heroism, and so forth, constitutes the *vibhāva* (the determinants).
The contraction and expansion occurring in the eyes constitute the *anubhāva* (the consequents).
The fusion of shame and longing is suggested;
likewise,
there is the commingling of emotions (bhāvaśabalatva).
The intermingling of entities that have entered into a relationship of the sublated and the sublator, or those that are indifferent.
That is to say, it is the state of being the object of a cognition that produces a single aesthetic wonder (*camatkṛti*).
An example:
"Alas, by me, a wretch, sin has been committed; for even a mere insect was driven away..."
"Alas, in the forest without me, that moon-faced woman—what life will she sustain?
How shall I look upon the faces of my virtuous friends, and what will they say to me?
Let the kingdom go to the netherworld; I have no desire to live this life again."

In this [verse], there is a complex intermingling (*śabalatā*) of the emotions of envy, dejection, despair, recollection, anxiety, shame, apprehension, and world-weariness, each arising from its own previously mentioned determinants (*vibhāva*).
As for what the commentators on the *Kāvyaprakāśa* have stated—that "complexity is the suppression of preceding emotions by succeeding ones"—that is not correct. [For example:
"Someone might see [her and say]: 'O you who are fickle, O restless one! What haste? I am a young maiden; give me support by the hand! Alas, alas! This is a transgression!'"

In the verse "kvāsi yāsi" (Where are you? Where are you going?), although there is not even a trace of the suppression of doubt, envy, fortitude, memory, fatigue, dejection, pride, and eagerness, their variegation (*śabalatā*) has been established by the author of the root text himself in the fifth chapter as a quality of the praise of the king;
however, the destruction produced by its own subsequent specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) is not suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
Nor is it expressible as a state of sublation, nor is it wondrous; therefore:
"In the mixing of coconut water, milk, sugar, and plantain..."
"The taste of entities is likewise distinct when they are combined.

Here, this should be understood: those paths (*dhvani*) of the cessation, emergence, junction, and commingling of emotional states (*bhāva*) that have been illustrated are also indeed *bhāva*-paths (*bhāvadhvani*).

This is because these emotional states—while being relished as if they were present—are being relished through such modes as being delimited by their arising, being in a state of perishing, being joined together, and being in a state of mutual co-location.
This is because primacy is appropriate [for the emotion] alone, since the aesthetic wonder (camatkṛti) rests precisely therein;
even though there are states related to it, such as its arising, destruction, conjunction, and variegation.
Since the status of being an object of aesthetic relish (*carvaṇā*) is equal [for both], it is not possible to determine primacy [between them];
nevertheless, because primacy has been established for the *bhāvas* (emotions) in their actual state,

and because it is appropriate to postulate that same primacy even when those very same *bhāvas*— such as the subsidence of emotion (*bhāvaśānti*) and so forth— are manifested through their opposition to tranquility and the like.

Furthermore, if it is accepted that in the case of the subsidence of emotion (*bhāvaśānti*) and so forth, the emotion is not primary, but rather the subsidence and so on are primary with the emotion as a subordinate element, then in those poetic works where emotions are manifested and their respective pacifications and so forth are expressed, there would be no status as *bhāvaśānti-dhvani* (suggestion of the subsidence of emotion) and the like. To explain: ... [The remainder of the passage follows] ...
"At dawn, as my beloved approached the dwelling of her rival,
a crimson glow quickly rose from the corners of the lotus-eyes of that fair-eyed woman.

Here, because the emergence of an emotion (*bhāvodaya*) is conveyed precisely through the verbal expression of the prefix *ut-* combined with the root *i* ("to go"), it constitutes the figure of speech *udāttālaṃkāra*.

If it is argued that even though the "arising" (*udaya*) is denotable, the status of being a *bhāva* remains well-established because the emotion itself is not denotable, [we reply]: this is not so, because if the primary element is unfit for designation, a designation based on a non-primary element is untenable.

In our view, however, although the arising is denotable, since the primary element—the indignation (*amarṣa*)—as delimited by that arising is not denotable, the designation of this as *bhāvodayadhvani* is indeed appropriate.

Thus, if tranquility (*praśama*) were to have as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) a state (*bhāva*) that is merely suggested (*vyajyamāna*), it could not constitute the suggestion of the subsiding of an emotion (*bhāvaśāntidhvani*). For example:
“When her lover fell at her feet—the very words for seeking forgiveness—the radiance of the reddened eyes of the lotus-eyed woman vanished.”

Now, since the pacification and so forth denoted by the words are invariably concomitant with the red luster itself, it follows that only the red luster, the pacification, and so on, are the expressed meanings;
it is not the pacification of anger and so forth, which are suggested by such [expressed] pacification and so on,
because the distinction between the suggester and the suggested is necessary.
Nor should it be argued that only the anger suggested by the redness is connected with the pacification and so forth that have become the expressed meaning;

for since the cognitions of the expressed and the suggested are established through a temporal sequence, it is impossible for the suggested to be connected with the expressed at the very moment when the connection of the expressed meanings is being understood.
Otherwise, there would be no syntactic connection for the phrase "of the corners of the lotus-eyes of Sudṛśī.
Not so;
even in this case—[it refers to] the gazelle-eyed woman who was banishing the fortitude of women and drinking in the beauty of Hari.

Even in such passages as, “The anger, though nourished by the memory of long-standing offenses, became a mere guest for a moment,” there would result the designation of *bhāvapraśama-dhvani* (the suggestion of the subsiding of an emotion),
because even if the emotion (*bhāva*) is directly expressed (*vācya*), its subsiding— which is the primary element— is suggested (*vyaṅgya*).

If it is argued that both [the states of tranquility and emergence] must be inexpressible, then, because tranquility and emergence were expressed by the terms "tranquility" (*śamatva*) and "emergence" (*udayatva*) in the two preceding verses, they would fail to serve as examples;
yet such an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) is certainly improper for sensitive critics (*sahṛdaya*).

Therefore, even in cases such as the subsidence of emotion (*bhāva-praśama*), it is the emotions themselves that possess primacy in producing aesthetic wonder (*camatkāritva*), while the subsidence and so forth are merely subordinate; hence, there is no fault of being a mere denoted meaning (*vācyatā-doṣa*) for that [subsidence].

This, moreover, is the cause for the difference in aesthetic wonder between the suggestion of emotions (*bhāva-dhvani*) and the suggestion of the subsidence of emotions (*bhāva-śānti-dhvani*) and so on: namely, that in one case, within the act of relish (*carvaṇā*), the emotions are characterized by indignation and the like delimited by their persistence.
Alternatively, the state of indignation (*amarṣa*) and so forth is itself the mode;
however, in other cases, states such as tranquility (*praśama*) may also occur.
But because a rasa is rooted in a permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), states such as tranquility are impossible [as its primary mode].
Or, if it were possible, there would be no sense of wonder;
thus, that is not investigated here.
This entire manifold of suggested meanings (vyaṅgyaprapañca), characterized by love (rati) and the rest, which has been described, [arises] instantaneously in a clear context.

When the determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*vyabhicārin*) have been perceived, they are apprehended by the most sensitive connoisseur through a subtle process of mental synthesis; because the sequence between cause and effect is thus unperceived, it is designated as "unperceived sequence" (*alakṣyakrama*).
However, where the context is such that it must be understood through deliberation...

Alternatively, the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth may be inferred; in that case, the slowness of the aesthetic wonder (*camatkṛti*) depends on the delay of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), and thus this [type of suggestion] also becomes one where the sequence is perceptible (*saṃlakṣyakrama*).
For example, in the previously cited verse beginning with "And she of delicate form, though lying upon the bed," the comprehension of the meaning of the word "now" (*saṃprati*) occurs with a delay.

Indeed, the status of being a suggestion where the sequence is imperceptible (*alakṣyakramavyaṅgya*) for *rasa* (such as love) and the like is not established merely by the cognition that apprehends the substratum (*dharmin*).
Therefore, in the context of suggestion where the sequence is perceptible (*lakṣyakrama*), it is said:
"While the divine sage was speaking thus, Pārvatī, standing by her father's side with her face cast down, began counting the petals of her play-lotus."

Thus, in this case, because even the counting of the petals of the play-lotus— characterized by downward-facing— becomes possible through the very nature of a young girl, and because there is a sense of wonder at her shame following her slight delay upon learning the circumstances of Nārada’s intervention regarding the marriage and so forth, this is a suggestion (*dhvani*) of sequential manifestation (*lakṣyakrama*).
Thus say the teacher Ānandavardhana:
"The meaning consisting of rasa, bhāva, and so forth, is only suggested (dhvanyamāna), not directly expressed (vācya).
Nevertheless, not every such instance falls within the scope of the 'suggestion of imperceptible sequence' (alakṣyakrama). So too say the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
It might be argued: if this [category of] rasa and so forth were the domain of that in which the sequence is perceptible (*saṃlakṣyakrama*),

then the statement of Abhinavagupta— "there are twelve varieties based on the power of the meaning (*arthaśaktimūla*)"— and the statement of Mammaṭa— "therefore, this [suggestion] consists of twelve types"— would not be consistent with the enumeration of the different kinds of resonance (*anuraṇana*).

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of eighteen types [of suggestion], because the suggested meanings— such as rasa and so forth— are manifested not only by the two kinds of denoted meaning (vastu and alaṃkāra), but also by the sixfold nature resulting from the three conditions of being "inherently possible" (*svataḥ-sambhavitva*), "established by the poet’s bold assertion" (*kavi-prauḍhokti-niṣpannatva*), and "established by the bold assertion of a character created by the poet" (*kavinibaddha-vaktr-prauḍhokti-niṣpannatva*). Thus, the suggested meaning would become eighteen-fold, just as the denoted meaning (vastu and alaṃkāra) itself becomes sixfold through those same three conditions.

To this it is replied: the stable emotion (sthāyibhāva), such as love (rati) and the like, becomes aesthetic flavor (rasa) only when manifested through clearly manifest determinants (vibhāva), consequents (anubhāva), and transitory states (vyabhicārin) in a manner where the sequence [of their cognition] is imperceptible, not by means of a perceptible sequence.
For "becoming rasa" indeed consists in the state of being a stable emotion that is the object of an extraordinary wonder arising instantaneously.

However, there is no contradiction with those [earlier] statements when one describes their intention as being that emotions such as love (*rati*), when manifested through a perceptible sequence (*saṃlakṣyakrama*), constitute merely a "fact" (*vastumātra*) and not a "rasa" or the like; yet,
the logical justification for this point must be investigated.

In the statement "the meaning consists of rasa, bhāva, and so forth," the terms *rasa* and so on refer to *rati* (love) and the like. Thus, they maintain that this aforementioned expansion of *rasa*-dhvani and the rest is manifested through words, phonemes, compositions, and sentences; through parts of words; and through those not consisting of phonemes, such as musical melodies (*rāga*) and the like. In this regard, although all words contained within a sentence are equally means for the cognition of the sentence-meaning by way of presenting their own individual meanings (*svārtha*), [only certain words] possess the capacity to produce aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) by virtue of being "active" (*kurvadrūpa*) and being delimited by the non-occurrence of such wonder.
Only a certain [quality] serves as the basis for the designation "sound" (*dhvani*),
as in the case of the word "slowly" (*mandam*) in the expression "he throws slowly.

Although it is easy to argue that for *racanā* (composition) and *varṇa* (phonemes), because they are contained within words and sentences, they merely enter the category of the delimiters of suggestiveness (*vyañjakatāvacchedaka*) and do not possess suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) itself, [this is not the case].

Nevertheless, the ancients maintain that since there is no decisive criterion (vinigamanāviraha) as to whether suggestiveness consists in being a specific arrangement of words and sentences, or in being words and sentences qualified by a specific arrangement, suggestiveness is established for each individual element— just as the causality of the staff, the wheel, and so forth is established individually with respect to a jar.

Specific arrangements of phonemes and word-structures possess the capacity to manifest qualities such as *mādhurya* (sweetness) and so forth, but not the capacity to manifest *rasa* (aesthetic flavor), due to their prolixity and lack of evidence. Indeed, there is no rule that the manifestation of qualities cannot occur without the manifestation of the possessor of those qualities (*guṇin*).
Because there is deviation [from the rule] in the case of the three sense organs;

and thus, just as the qualities (guṇas) of a substance (guṇin)— whether brought forth by their respective manifestors, or neutral, and whether through mutual contact or in isolation— become objects of their respective cognitions, so too, according to the Neo-Naiyāyikas, do the rasas and their qualities become objects of manifestation.

As for the examples, those such as "tāṃ tamāla... and so forth have already been mentioned above regarding the suggestiveness of a sentence; and regarding the suggestiveness of a verse-quarter, there is also "āvirbhūtā yad avadhi... and so forth.

Regarding the suggestiveness of an entire composition (*prabandha*), however, well-known illustrations are the *Yogavāsiṣṭha-rāmāyaṇa* for the suggestion of the peaceful (*śānta*) and compassionate (*karuṇa*) sentiments, and works such as the *Ratnāvalī* for the suggestion of the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) sentiment.
And five waves of meaning are produced from a single word-part,
such as in the case of the taddhita suffix *karu* in the expression “I carry this entire universe-egg,” which was previously cited as an example of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*).
Likewise, when passion and so forth are also suggested, the authority for their existence lies solely in the hearts of the sensitive connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*).

Thus, examples of these [elements], such as rasa and the rest, have been described primarily. However, their subordination and their names will be discussed later. In that regard, it is only when they are predominant that they possess the nature of rasa and so forth.
Otherwise, however, they are simply passion (*rati*) and so forth.

Some say that although the word "rasa" appears in the names [of the dramatic sentiments], it actually refers to passion and the like. [Yet others argue] that the status of being "rasa" and so forth certainly exists.
However, others maintain that it does not serve as the basis for the designation "dhvani."
